<question>
If CLIP is zero-shot, why do the authors say their evaluation isn't really a true zero-shot setup?

chosen.content:
The model is never trained on the downstream datasets. The leak is in the *research process*: model selection was guided by labeled data from the target tasks.

The first issue is validation-set feedback. Although the work focuses on zero-shot transfer, the authors "repeatedly queried performance on full validation sets to guide the development of CLIP" [S1]. These sets often contain thousands of labeled examples, which a genuine zero-shot user would never have [S1]. Every architecture, prompt, or training decision made by checking those numbers works like implicit hyperparameter tuning on the target distribution. Reported zero-shot accuracy therefore carries an optimistic bias from that selection loop. The authors note that the same concern has been raised in semi-supervised learning [S1], where tuning on large labeled validation sets undercuts claims of label efficiency.

The second issue is benchmark co-adaptation. Results on Kornblith et al.'s 12-dataset suite are reported as a standardized collection, but the main results use "a somewhat haphazardly assembled collection of 27 datasets that is undeniably co-adapted with the development and capabilities of CLIP" [S1]. The benchmark and the model evolved together. Dataset inclusion may have tracked what CLIP could do, which inflates apparent breadth of transfer, not just the per-task numbers.

The authors' proposed fix is a new benchmark built explicitly to evaluate broad zero-shot transfer, rather than repurposed supervised datasets [S1]. Such a benchmark would separate held-out evaluation from development, and select tasks without reference to the model's strengths.

rejected.content:
The model itself is zero-shot, but the *process of building it* was not. While developing CLIP, the authors kept checking its scores on large sets of labeled examples, and that gave them information a real zero-shot user would never have.

Three ideas, as general background rather than the paper's own text, make this clearer:

- **Zero-shot transfer** means using a model on a new task without giving it any labeled examples of that task. For CLIP, you just describe the categories in words (like "a photo of a dog"), and it picks the best match.
- **Validation set overfitting**: researchers keep a pile of labeled examples aside to check how well their model is doing. If they check it again and again and adjust their choices each time, the model slowly gets tuned to that particular pile. It's like a student who keeps retaking the same practice exam: their score climbs partly because they've learned that exam, not just the subject.
- **Benchmark co-adaptation**: the tests and the model shape each other. If you pick which tests to report while you're building the model, you may lean, even without meaning to, toward tests your model happens to be good at.

The authors admit to the first problem directly. They say that "despite our focus on zero-shot transfer, we repeatedly queried performance on full validation sets to guide the development of CLIP" [S1]. Those validation sets "often have thousands of examples," which they call "unrealistic for true zero-shot scenarios" [S1]. Someone truly facing a brand-new task wouldn't have thousands of labeled examples to steer by. They note that researchers in semi-supervised learning, a related area that also works with very little labeled data, have raised the same concern [S1].

The second problem is how the test datasets were chosen. The authors did report results on a standard 12-dataset collection from earlier work [S1]. But their main results use "a somewhat haphazardly assembled collection of 27 datasets" that they say is "undeniably co-adapted with the development and capabilities of CLIP" [S1]. In other words, the test collection grew alongside the model, so it may flatter CLIP a bit.

Their proposed fix is a new benchmark built specifically to test broad zero-shot ability, instead of reusing existing datasets that were originally made for ordinary training with labels [S1]. A test designed in advance, and not tuned to during development, would give a fairer picture of how CLIP does on tasks it has truly never seen.

Superficially, DenseNets are quite similar to ResNets: Eq. (2) differs from Eq. (1) only in that the inputs to H_l(·) are concatenated instead of summed. However, the implications of this seemingly small modification lead to substantially different behaviors of the two network architectures.

Model compactness. As a direct consequence of the input concatenation, the feature-maps learned by any of the DenseNet layers can be accessed by all subsequent layers. This encourages feature reuse throughout the network, and leads to more compact models.

The left two plots in Figure 4 show the result of an experiment that aims to compare the parameter efficiency of all variants of DenseNets (left) and also a comparable ResNet architecture (middle). We train multiple small networks with varying depths on C10+ and plot their test accuracies as a function of network parameters. In comparison with other popular network architectures, such as AlexNet [16] or VGG-net [29], ResNets with pre-activation use fewer parameters while typically achieving better results [12]. The graph shows that DenseNet-BC is consistently the most parameter efficient variant of DenseNet. The right plot in Figure 4 shows that a DenseNet-BC with only 0.8M trainable parameters is able to achieve comparable accuracy as the 1001-layer (pre-activation) ResNet [12] with 10.2M parameters.

Implicit Deep Supervision. One explanation for the improved accuracy of dense convolutional networks may be that individual layers receive additional supervision from the loss function through the shorter connections. One can interpret DenseNets to perform a kind of “deep supervision”. The benefits of deep supervision have previously been shown in deeply-supervised nets (DSN; [20]), which have classifiers attached to every hidden layer, enforcing the intermediate layers to learn discriminative features.

<question>
How much more parameter-efficient is DenseNet compared to ResNet on CIFAR-10 — like, how many params do you need for the same accuracy?
</question>

chosen.content:
On C10+, DenseNet-BC needs about **1/3 of the parameters** of a pre-activation ResNet to reach the same test accuracy [S2]. The authors measure this by training several small networks of varying depth for each family and plotting test accuracy against parameter count. They compare DenseNet ($k=12$) against pre-activation ResNets because those already beat AlexNet and VGG on parameter efficiency [S2]. DenseNet-BC is also the most parameter-efficient of the DenseNet variants [S2].

At the extreme end, a 100-layer DenseNet-BC with 0.8M parameters matches the accuracy of the 1001-layer pre-activation ResNet, which has 10.2M parameters [S1][S2]. That is roughly a 12–13× reduction for that pair, much larger than the ~3× trend across the small-model sweep. The figure caption describes the ResNet only as "more than 10M parameters" [S1], and the 10.2M figure comes from the Discussion [S2].

The authors attribute the compactness to concatenation rather than summation. Every layer's feature maps stay directly accessible to all later layers, which encourages feature reuse [S2]. They say the C10+ result is consistent with ImageNet, where Figure 3 plots top-1 single-crop validation error against both learned parameters and test-time FLOPs [S1][S2]. These passages only describe the figures, so they give no exact error rates for either the CIFAR sweep or the ImageNet curves. For those you would need to read the plots or the results tables.

rejected.content:
DenseNet-BC needs about **one third** of the parameters of a comparable ResNet to reach the same accuracy on CIFAR-10 [S2]. Some background makes that number clearer.

A **parameter** is one adjustable number inside a network, a "knob" the network tunes while it learns. Parameter count is a rough measure of a model's size and memory cost. **Parameter efficiency** asks how much accuracy you get per knob. This is general background rather than something the paper defines.

A ResNet is a deep image-recognition network whose layers add their input back onto their output, like passing along your notes plus your own corrections. "Pre-activation" is a refined version of ResNet that reorders some steps inside each layer. The paper uses it as its comparison point because it already uses fewer parameters than older designs like AlexNet or VGG while getting better results [S2].

DenseNet differs in one main way. Instead of adding earlier results together, each layer stacks (concatenates) all earlier layers' outputs side by side, so any later layer can reach anything computed before it [S2]. The authors argue this lets layers reuse features instead of relearning them, which makes the models more compact [S2]. DenseNet-BC is the slimmed-down variant, and it was the most parameter-efficient DenseNet they tested [S2].

The paper doesn't spell out how the "B" (bottleneck) and "C" (compression) parts work in these passages. In general terms, both are tricks to keep each layer's data narrow, so the network needs fewer knobs.

The authors trained many small networks of different depths on C10+ and plotted accuracy against parameter count. To hit the same accuracy, DenseNet-BC needed roughly 1/3 the parameters of the pre-activation ResNets [S1][S2]. C10+ is CIFAR-10, a dataset of small 10-category images; in general, the "+" means the training images are augmented with simple shifts and flips.

The extreme example is striking. A 100-layer DenseNet-BC with only 0.8M parameters reaches accuracy comparable to a 1001-layer pre-activation ResNet with 10.2M parameters [S1][S2]. That is about 13 times fewer parameters for similar accuracy.

The same pattern holds on the much larger ImageNet dataset. There, the comparison is plotted against both parameter count and test-time computation (FLOPs, the number of arithmetic operations needed to classify an image) [S1][S2]. These passages only describe the figures, so the exact error rates for any of these comparisons aren't given here; you'd need to read them off Figures 3 and 4.

Most standard image classification datasets treat the information naming or describing classes which enables natural language based zero-shot transfer as an afterthought. The vast majority of datasets annotate images with just a numeric id of the label and contain a file mapping these ids back to their names in English. Some datasets, such as Flowers102 and GTSRB, don’t appear to include this mapping at all in their released versions preventing zero-shot transfer entirely.^2 For many datasets, we observed these labels may be shot performance. Compared to the baseline of using contextless class names, prompt engineering and ensembling boost zero-shot classification performance by almost 5 points on average across 36 datasets. A common issue is polysemy. When the name of a class is the only information provided to CLIP’s text encoder it is unable to differentiate which word sense is meant due to the lack of context. In some cases multiple meanings of the same word might be included as different classes in the same dataset! This happens in ImageNet which contains both construction cranes and cranes that fly. Another example is found in classes of the Oxford-IIIT Pet dataset where the word boxer is, from context, clearly referring to a breed of dog, but to a text encoder lacking context could just as likely refer to a type of athlete.

<question>
Is the jump from 11.5% to 76.2% on ImageNet over Visual N-Grams actually a fair comparison, or is CLIP just using way more data and compute?

chosen.content:
Not as a methods comparison, and the authors say so themselves: Table 1 is "meant for contextualizing the performance of CLIP and should not be interpreted as a direct methods comparison," because many performance-relevant differences were not controlled for [S1].

Three ideas help in reading the table:

- **Zero-shot transfer**: classifying a dataset's images without training on any of its labeled examples. For CLIP, the class names (e.g. via a template like "A photo of a {label}.") go through the text encoder and act as the classifier [S2]. That is how CLIP reaches 76.2% on ImageNet using none of its 1.28 million labeled training examples [S1].
- **Contrastive image-text pretraining**: as general background, rather than something these passages spell out, the model learns separate image and text encoders so that matching (image, caption) pairs get high similarity and mismatched pairs within a batch get low similarity. Zero-shot classification then picks the class prompt whose embedding is most similar to the image's embedding.
- **Top-1 vs top-5 accuracy**: also general background. Top-1 counts a prediction correct only if the highest-scoring class is right. Top-5 counts it correct if the right class is anywhere in the five highest. The paper notes CLIP's top-5 is noticeably higher than its top-1, reaching 95% [S1].

The headline gap comes with these uncontrolled differences relative to Visual N-Grams [S1]:

- a training dataset 10x larger
- a vision model needing nearly 100x more compute per prediction
- likely over 1000x the training compute
- a transformer-based model, an architecture that did not exist when Visual N-Grams was published

So much of the jump from 11.5% to 76.2% could come from scale and four years of progress rather than the training objective.

For a closer comparison, the authors trained a CLIP ResNet-50 on the same YFCC100M dataset Visual N-Grams used. It matched Visual N-Grams' reported ImageNet performance within one V100 GPU day [S1]. This baseline was trained from scratch, while Visual N-Grams was initialized from ImageNet-pretrained weights [S1]. Matching the same number with less help and little compute suggests the CLIP objective is more efficient on its own. Still, this is a match at a low accuracy, not evidence that the method alone produces the 76.2%.

Because a three-dataset comparison against one prior system can't carry much weight, the authors expanded the evaluation to over 30 datasets and compared against over 50 existing computer vision systems [S1].

rejected.content:
Not as a methods comparison, and the authors say so explicitly. Table 1 is meant to contextualize CLIP's performance and "should not be interpreted as a direct methods comparison," because many performance-relevant differences were not controlled for [S1]. The 11.5% → 76.2% gap [S1] mixes several confounds:

- **Data:** a training set 10x larger [S1].
- **Inference cost:** a vision model needing nearly 100x more compute per prediction [S1].
- **Training compute:** likely over 1000x what Visual N-Grams used [S1].
- **Architecture:** a transformer-based model, which did not exist when Visual N-Grams was published [S1].

The closer control matches the data. A CLIP ResNet-50 trained on the same YFCC100M dataset matched Visual N-Grams' reported ImageNet accuracy within one V100 GPU day [S1]. The control also handicaps CLIP, since it was trained from scratch while Visual N-Grams was initialized from ImageNet-pretrained weights [S1]. This shows the contrastive objective reaching the old result very efficiently, with no ImageNet supervision leaking in through initialization. It is not evidence that the objective alone explains the 76.2%. The paper doesn't isolate how much of the full gap comes from each factor.

Because three datasets and one prior system make a weak test, the authors expanded the evaluation to over 30 datasets and over 50 existing computer vision systems (Appendix A) [S1]. That broader suite is the better basis for judging CLIP's zero-shot transfer.

We proposed a new convolutional network architecture, which we refer to as Dense Convolutional Network (DenseNet). It introduces direct connections between any two layers with the same feature-map size. We showed that DenseNets scale naturally to hundreds of layers, while exhibiting no optimization difficulties. In our experiments, DenseNets tend to yield consistent improvement in accuracy with growing number of parameters, without any signs of performance degradation or overfitting. Under multiple settings, it achieved state-of-the-art results across several highly competitive datasets. Whilst following a simple connectivity rule, DenseNets naturally integrate the properties of identity mappings, deep supervision, and diversified depth. They allow feature reuse throughout the networks and can consequently learn more compact and, according to our experiments, more accurate models. Because of their compact internal representations and reduced feature redundancy, DenseNets may be good feature extractors for various computer vision tasks that build on convolutional features, e.g., [4, 5]. The authors didn't tune DenseNet's training setup for DenseNet. They borrowed settings tuned for a different architecture, so the reported numbers likely understate what DenseNets can do.

The paper takes the following training concepts as known; here is the general background:

- **Hyperparameter tuning** means searching over the settings you choose before training, such as weight decay, batch size, number of epochs and initial learning rate. Settings that work well for one model are not guaranteed to be best for another.
- A **learning rate schedule** says how the step size changes during training. A common pattern starts large and drops by a constant factor at fixed epochs. When and how much to drop it can noticeably change final accuracy.
- **Residual networks** (ResNets) add skip connections of the form $x_{\ell} = H_\ell(x_{\ell-1}) + x_{\ell-1}$. They were the dominant deep CNN baseline when DenseNet appeared, so well-tuned training recipes already existed for them.

The authors state that they "adopted hyperparameter settings optimized for residual networks" in their study [S1]. Because of this, they expect that "further gains in accuracy of DenseNets may be obtained by more detailed tuning of hyperparameters and learning rate schedules" [S1]. DenseNet's connectivity is different from ResNet's: each layer receives the feature maps of all earlier layers in the block. A recipe tuned for ResNets is therefore a reasonable starting point but probably not the best one.

Their scaling results support this view. DenseNets "tend to yield consistent improvement in accuracy with growing number of parameters, without any signs of performance degradation or overfitting" [S1]. If accuracy is still rising as models grow, and nothing points to the method hitting a ceiling, the reported results look like a lower bound rather than the limit of the architecture [S1]. DenseNets also scale to hundreds of layers "while exhibiting no optimization difficulties" [S1]. That suggests better training settings could be exploited rather than fighting instability.

The main reason is that the authors never tuned their training settings for DenseNet itself. They borrowed settings that had been tuned for a different kind of network [S1]. A few general ideas, which the paper takes as known, make it clear why that matters.

As general background, training a neural network involves choices made by people before training starts: how long to train, how big each learning step is, and so on. These choices are called **hyperparameters**, and "tuning" them means trying different values to find the ones that work best for a particular network. Settings that suit one network are not guaranteed to suit another, much like a recipe's oven temperature may need adjusting for a different oven.

One especially important hyperparameter is the learning rate, which is how big a step the network takes each time it corrects its mistakes. In general, a **learning rate schedule** is a plan for changing that step size during training, often starting with big steps to make fast progress and switching to small steps later to fine-tune. A poorly matched schedule can leave a network short of its best accuracy.

Residual networks (ResNets) are an earlier, very popular family of image-recognition networks. Their key feature, described here as general background, is "shortcut" connections that let information skip over layers. Because ResNets were widely used, good training settings for them were already well known.

The paper explains that it adopted "hyperparameter settings optimized for residual networks" rather than settings chosen for DenseNet [S1]. Because of this, the authors believe DenseNet's accuracy could improve further with "more detailed tuning of hyperparameters and learning rate schedules" [S1]. In other words, DenseNet got strong results while working with borrowed settings, which suggests its reported numbers are not its ceiling.

A second clue supports this. In their experiments, DenseNets kept getting more accurate as the authors made them bigger (gave them more adjustable parameters), "without any signs of performance degradation or overfitting" [S1]. Overfitting is when a network memorizes its training examples instead of learning patterns that carry over to new images. Since adding size kept helping and nothing started to break down, the authors had not yet hit a limit, which points to remaining room for improvement [S1].

If CLIP is zero-shot, why do the authors say their evaluation isn't really a true zero-shot setup?

chosen.content:
The model itself is zero-shot, but the *process of building it* was not. While developing CLIP, the authors kept checking its scores on large sets of labeled examples, and that gave them information a real zero-shot user would never have.

Three ideas, as general background rather than the paper's own text, make this clearer:

- **Zero-shot transfer** means using a model on a new task without giving it any labeled examples of that task. For CLIP, you just describe the categories in words (like "a photo of a dog"), and it picks the best match.
- **Validation set overfitting**: researchers keep a pile of labeled examples aside to check how well their model is doing. If they check it again and again and adjust their choices each time, the model slowly gets tuned to that particular pile. It's like a student who keeps retaking the same practice exam: their score climbs partly because they've learned that exam, not just the subject.
- **Benchmark co-adaptation**: the tests and the model shape each other. If you pick which tests to report while you're building the model, you may lean, even without meaning to, toward tests your model happens to be good at.

The authors admit to the first problem directly. They say that "despite our focus on zero-shot transfer, we repeatedly queried performance on full validation sets to guide the development of CLIP" [S1]. Those validation sets "often have thousands of examples," which they call "unrealistic for true zero-shot scenarios" [S1]. Someone truly facing a brand-new task wouldn't have thousands of labeled examples to steer by. They note that researchers in semi-supervised learning, a related area that also works with very little labeled data, have raised the same concern [S1].

The second problem is how the test datasets were chosen. The authors did report results on a standard 12-dataset collection from earlier work [S1]. But their main results use "a somewhat haphazardly assembled collection of 27 datasets" that they say is "undeniably co-adapted with the development and capabilities of CLIP" [S1]. In other words, the test collection grew alongside the model, so it may flatter CLIP a bit.

Their proposed fix is a new benchmark built specifically to test broad zero-shot ability, instead of reusing existing datasets that were originally made for ordinary training with labels [S1]. A test designed in advance, and not tuned to during development, would give a fairer picture of how CLIP does on tasks it has truly never seen.

rejected.content:
The model is never trained on the downstream datasets. The leak is in the *research process*: model selection was guided by labeled data from the target tasks.

The first issue is validation-set feedback. Although the work focuses on zero-shot transfer, the authors "repeatedly queried performance on full validation sets to guide the development of CLIP" [S1]. These sets often contain thousands of labeled examples, which a genuine zero-shot user would never have [S1]. Every architecture, prompt, or training decision made by checking those numbers works like implicit hyperparameter tuning on the target distribution. Reported zero-shot accuracy therefore carries an optimistic bias from that selection loop. The authors note that the same concern has been raised in semi-supervised learning [S1], where tuning on large labeled validation sets undercuts claims of label efficiency.

The second issue is benchmark co-adaptation. Results on Kornblith et al.'s 12-dataset suite are reported as a standardized collection, but the main results use "a somewhat haphazardly assembled collection of 27 datasets that is undeniably co-adapted with the development and capabilities of CLIP" [S1]. The benchmark and the model evolved together. Dataset inclusion may have tracked what CLIP could do, which inflates apparent breadth of transfer, not just the per-task numbers.

The authors' proposed fix is a new benchmark built explicitly to evaluate broad zero-shot transfer, rather than repurposed supervised datasets [S1]. Such a benchmark would separate held-out evaluation from development, and select tasks without reference to the model's strengths.

<question>
When they say CLIP got state of the art on 21 of 27 datasets in linear probes, does that mean it had the single highest score, or something looser?
</question>

chosen.content:
Looser. "State of the art" here means CLIP ViT-L/14 at 336×336 pixels scored inside a statistical confidence interval around each dataset's top score, not that it had the strictly highest number on all 21 datasets [S1].

In general, a **linear probe** evaluation freezes a pretrained model, extracts its features for each image, and trains only a linear classifier (such as logistic regression) on top. The accuracy of that classifier measures how linearly separable, and so how useful, the frozen representation is. This is general background on the method, not a definition taken from the paper.

Also general background: a test-set accuracy is an estimate from a finite sample, so it carries uncertainty. A confidence interval gives the range of true accuracies consistent with the observed score. A 99.5% interval is wide enough that a score inside it can't be confidently separated from the top score. The Clopper-Pearson interval is an exact interval for a binomial proportion, such as the fraction of test images classified correctly. It is computed from the binomial distribution itself rather than from a normal approximation, so it stays valid for small test sets and for accuracies near 0% or 100%.

The authors draw a Clopper-Pearson 99.5% interval around each dataset's best score. If CLIP's score falls inside it, CLIP counts as state of the art for that dataset [S1]. These scores are the ones printed in bold in Table 10 [S1]. CLIP can therefore be slightly below the best number and still count. In Table 10, for example, the L/14-336px row has 97.9 in its second column while the L/14 row has 98.0 [S2]. Test-set size also matters: the test sets range from 500 images (CLEVR Counts, Hateful Memes) to 50,000 (ImageNet) [S1]. On small test sets the interval is wide, so a fairly large gap can still fall inside it.

The authors still read the results as a strong win. On many datasets CLIP performs significantly better than the other models, which they take as evidence that natural language supervision beats pre-training on image classification [S1]. Section 3.2 discusses the linear probe results further [S1].

rejected.content:
Something looser. "State of the art" here means CLIP ViT-L/14@336px scored inside the Clopper-Pearson 99.5% confidence interval around each dataset's top score [S1]. So on some of those 21 datasets another model may have the single highest number, and CLIP still counts because its score is statistically indistinguishable from it at that confidence level.

You can see this in the raw rows. On CIFAR-10, for example, L/14 at 224px has 98.0 and L/14-336px has 97.9 [S2]. A strict "highest score" criterion would not credit the 336px model there, but the interval criterion does.

The protocol is the standard **linear probe**: the pre-trained encoder is frozen, and a linear classifier is trained on its features for each of the 27 datasets [S1]. It measures how linearly separable the representation is, not how well the full network performs after fine-tuning.

In Table 10, the scores that fall inside each dataset's 99.5% interval are shown in bold [S1]. A dataset can therefore have several bolded entries, and the "21 of 27" counts the datasets where the best CLIP model is among them.

The authors also point out that on many datasets CLIP's margin is large, not just a tie within the interval. They read this as evidence that natural language supervision beats traditional pre-training based on image classification [S1].

The paper doesn't spell out how the Clopper-Pearson interval is computed for metrics that aren't simple proportions, such as 11-point mAP, mean-per-class accuracy, or ROC AUC. The interval is naturally defined for binomial accuracy, so for those metrics the "within CI" call is presumably an approximation.

We train a series of 5 ResNets and 3 Vision Transformers. For the ResNets we train a ResNet-50, a ResNet-101, and then 3 more which follow EfficientNet-style model scaling and use approximately 4x, 16x, and 64x the compute of a ResNet-50. They are denoted as RN50x4, RN50x16, and RN50x64 respectively. For the Vision Transformers we train a ViT-B/32, a ViT-B/16, and a ViT-L/14. We train all models for 32 epochs. We use the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2014) with decoupled weight decay regularization (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) applied to all weights that are not gains or biases, and decay the learning rate using a cosine schedule (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2016). Initial hyperparameters were set using a combination of grid searches, random search, and manual tuning on the baseline ResNet-50 model when trained for 1 epoch. Hyper-parameters were then adapted heuristically for larger models due to computational constraints. The learnable temperature parameter τ was initialized to the equivalent of 0.07 from (Wu et al., 2018) and clipped to prevent scaling the logits by more than 100 which we found necessary to prevent training instability. We use a very large minibatch size of 32,768. Mixed-precision (Micikevicius et al., 2017) was used to accelerate training and save memory. To save additional memory, gradient checkpointing (Griewank & Walther, 2000; Chen et al., 2016), half-precision Adam statistics (Dhariwal et al., 2020), and half-precision stochastically rounded text encoder weights were used. The calculation of embedding similarities was also sharded with individual GPUs computing only the subset of the pairwise similarities necessary for their local batch of embeddings. The largest ResNet model, RN50x64, took 18 days to train on 592 V100 GPUs while the largest Vision Transformer took 12 days on 256 V100 GPUs. For the ViT-L/14 we also pre-train at a higher 336 pixel resolution for one additional epoch to boost performance similar to FixRes (Touvron et al., 2019). We denote this model as ViT-L/14@336px. Unless otherwise specified, all results reported in this paper as “CLIP” use this model which we found to perform best.

chosen.content:
On the image side, CLIP follows the compound-scaling result of EfficientNet. That work found that spreading extra compute across width, depth and input resolution beats putting it into a single axis, which is how earlier vision work typically scaled: width alone or depth alone [S1]. CLIP keeps the idea but not EfficientNet's tuned per-axis ratios. It uses a simple baseline that splits the added compute **equally** among width, depth and resolution [S1]. This scheme produces the RN50x4, RN50x16 and RN50x64 models, at roughly 4x, 16x and 64x the compute of a ResNet-50 [S2].

The text transformer gets a much cheaper treatment. Its width is scaled in proportion to the computed increase in ResNet width, and its depth is not scaled at all [S1]. The stated reason is empirical: the authors found CLIP's performance to be less sensitive to text encoder capacity [S1]. Compute therefore goes where it pays off, into the vision tower, and the text encoder only widens enough to stay matched to the image side.

The paper gives no deeper explanation for this insensitivity, and it reports no ablation in these passages. One plausible reading, as general background rather than the paper's claim, is that captions are short and the contrastive objective mostly needs a sentence-level embedding. The visual side has to do the harder perceptual work, so extra text-encoder depth adds little.

rejected.content:
CLIP has two parts: an **image encoder** that turns a picture into a list of numbers, and a text encoder that does the same for a caption. Making a model bigger gives it more computing power, or "compute," to work with. The question is where to spend that extra compute, and the answer is different for the two parts.

Some general background, which the paper takes as known, is needed first. Picture a model as a stack of processing layers, like floors in a building:

1. **Compound scaling** means growing a model along several "dials" at once instead of turning just one. The three dials are below.
2. **Width vs. depth**: width is how much each floor can handle at once (a wider floor holds more workers). Depth is how many floors are stacked (more steps of processing, one after another).
3. **Input resolution** is how detailed the picture fed into the model is. More pixels show finer details but take more work to process.

On the image side, earlier vision research usually grew models along just one dial, making them only wider or only deeper [S1]. The CLIP authors instead borrowed an idea from the EfficientNet work. That work found that spreading extra compute across width, depth *and* resolution together beats pouring it all into one dial [S1]. A balanced approach makes sense here. A deeper, wider model gains little if the image is too blurry to show the details it could learn from, and a sharper image is wasted on a model too small to use it.

The EfficientNet work carefully tuned how much compute each dial gets. CLIP skips that tuning and simply splits the extra compute equally among the three, as a "simple baseline" [S1]. This is how the larger image models, RN50x4, RN50x16 and RN50x64, were built, using roughly 4, 16 and 64 times the compute of the base ResNet-50 [S2].

On the text side, the authors grow only the width. They make the text encoder wider in step with how much wider the image model got, and they leave its depth unchanged [S1]. Their reason is practical. They found CLIP's performance was "less sensitive to the capacity of the text encoder" [S1]. In other words, giving the text side more power didn't help much, so spending extra compute there was not worth it. Resolution doesn't apply to text, since a caption has no pixels.

The paper doesn't explain *why* the text side matters less. It reports this as something the authors observed.

Large language models. A variety of large language models have been introduced in the last few years. These include both dense transformer models (Brown et al., 2020; Lieber et al., 2021; Rae et al., 2021; Smith et al., 2022; Thoppilan et al., 2022) and mixture-of-expert (MoE) models (Du et al., 2021; Fedus et al., 2021; Zoph et al., 2022). The drive to train larger and larger models is clear—so far increasing the size of language models has been responsible for improving the state-of-the-art in many language modelling tasks. Nonetheless, large language models face several challenges, including their overwhelming computational requirements (the cost of training and inference increase with model size) (Rae et al., 2021; Thoppilan et al., 2022) and the need for acquiring more high-quality training data. Modelling the scaling behavior. Understanding the scaling behaviour of language models and their transfer properties has been important in the development of recent large models (Hernandez et al., 2021; Kaplan et al., 2020). Kaplan et al. (2020) first showed a predictable relationship between model size and loss over many orders of magnitude. The authors investigate the question of choosing the optimal model size to train for a given compute budget. Similar to us, they address this question by training various models. Our work differs from Kaplan et al. (2020) in several important ways. First, the authors use a fixed number of training tokens and learning rate schedule for all models; this prevents them from modelling the impact of these hyperparameters on the loss. For a fixed learning rate cosine schedule to 130B tokens, the intermediate loss estimates (for D^{′} << 130B) are therefore overestimates of the loss of a model trained with a schedule length matching D^{′}. Using these intermediate losses results in underestimating the effectiveness of training models on less data than 130B tokens, and eventually contributes to the conclusion that model size should increase faster than training data size as compute budget increases. In contrast, our analysis predicts that both quantities should scale at roughly the same rate. Secondly, we include models with up to 16B parameters, as we observe that there is slight curvature in the FLOP-loss frontier (see Appendix E)—in fact, the majority of the models used in our analysis have more than 500 million parameters, in contrast the majority of runs in Kaplan et al. chosen.content:
The authors grant the premise: so far, increasing language model size has been responsible for improving the state of the art in many language modelling tasks, and the largest dense transformers have passed 500 billion parameters [S1]. They name two challenges that push back against scaling parameters alone [S1]:

- **Compute.** The cost of both training and inference grows with model size [S1]. The inference cost matters as much as the training cost. A larger model is more expensive every time it is served, not only once during pretraining.
- **Data.** Continued scaling requires acquiring more high-quality training data [S1]. Parameter count does not substitute for this; the data has to come from somewhere.

The passage ends with the authors' claim that "larger, high quality datasets will play a key role in any further scaling of language models" [S1]. That sentence foreshadows the paper's main finding, which is developed later in the paper rather than in this section.

rejected.content:
The paper agrees that bigger has worked so far. Two kinds of model are involved, and one idea ties them together:

- **Dense transformer**: the standard kind of language model, where every one of its internal numbers (its "parameters", the dials it tunes while learning) is used for every word it processes. The paper lists several of these models, and the largest have passed 500 billion parameters [S1].
- **Mixture of experts**: a different design the paper also mentions [S1]. Instead of one big model, it holds many smaller "expert" sub-models and sends each word to only a few of them. It is like a hospital where a patient sees two specialists rather than every doctor. The paper names this design but doesn't describe how it works, so this description is general background.
- **Scaling laws**: earlier work found a predictable relationship between a model's size and its error ("loss") across a huge range of sizes [S2]. This is why making models bigger felt like a reliable recipe.

Following that recipe, increasing model size has been responsible for improving the best results on many language tasks [S1]. The authors name two obstacles to simply continuing.

1. **Cost.** The cost of training and of inference grows with model size [S1]. Inference means actually using the model once it is trained.
2. **Data.** Large models need more high-quality training text, and that text has to be gathered [S1].

Size alone doesn't make a model smart, which is why data matters. The parameters are where knowledge gets stored, and that knowledge comes from the text the model reads during training. This explanation is general background, not a claim from this passage. A useful picture is a huge library with too few books to fill it. Adding shelves doesn't help much if there's nothing new to put on them.

The passage ends with the key hint: the authors say that "larger, high quality datasets will play a key role in any further scaling of language models" [S1]. This line is only foreshadowing here. It points ahead to the paper's main finding, which later sections develop: the field has been growing model size while neglecting how much data those models are trained on.

Capacity. Without compression or bottleneck layers, there is a general trend that DenseNets perform better as L and k increase. We attribute this primarily to the corresponding growth in model capacity. This is best demonstrated by the column of C10+ and C100+. On C10+, the error drops from 5.24% to 4.10% and finally to 3.74% as the number of parameters increases from 1.0M, over 7.0M to 27.2M. On C100+, we observe a similar trend. This suggests that DenseNets can utilize the increased representational power of bigger and deeper models. It also indicates that they do not suffer from overfitting or the optimization difficulties of residual networks [11].

Parameter Efficiency. The results in Table 2 indicate that DenseNets utilize parameters more efficiently than alternative architectures (in particular, ResNets). The DenseNet-BC with bottleneck structure and dimension reduction at transition layers is particularly parameter-efficient. For example, our 250-layer model only has 15.3M parameters, but it consistently outperforms other models such as FractalNet and Wide ResNets that have more than 30M parameters. 4.4. Classification Results on ImageNet

We evaluate DenseNet-BC with different depths and growth rates on the ImageNet classification task, and compare it with state-of-the-art ResNet architectures. To ensure a fair comparison between the two architectures, we eliminate all other factors such as differences in data preprocessing and optimization settings by adopting the publicly available Torch implementation for ResNet by [8]^1. We simply replace the ResNet model with the DenseNet-BC network, and keep all the experiment settings exactly the same as those used for ResNet.

We report the single-crop and 10-crop validation errors of DenseNets on ImageNet in Table 3. Figure 3 shows the single-crop top-1 validation errors of DenseNets and ResNets as a function of the number of parameters (left) and FLOPs (right). The results presented in the figure reveal that DenseNets perform on par with the state-of-the-art ResNets, whilst requiring significantly fewer parameters and computation to achieve comparable performance. The 1001-layer ResNet gets lower training loss than the 100-layer DenseNet-BC but about the same test error — what does that tell us?

chosen.content:
The ResNet fits the training data more tightly but gets no better on held-out data, so more of its fit is memorisation. DenseNet-BC reaches the same test error with a much smaller model, which suggests it uses its parameters more efficiently and is less prone to overfitting.

Three pieces of general background, not taken from the passages, help read the comparison:

- The **generalization gap** is test error minus training error. Two models with equal test error but different training loss have different gaps, and the one with the lower training loss has the larger gap.
- The growth rate $k$ is the number of feature maps each DenseNet layer adds to the shared stack. Raising $k$ widens every layer and quickly multiplies the parameter count.
- Bottleneck layers put a $1\times1$ convolution in front of each $3\times3$ convolution to cut the input channels. Compression shrinks the channel count at transition layers.

DenseNet-BC is the variant with the "bottleneck structure and dimension reduction at transition layers" [S1]. With $L=100$ and $k=12$ it matches the 1001-layer pre-activation ResNet: 4.51% vs 4.62% error on C10+ and 22.27% vs 22.71% on C100+. It does this "using 90% fewer parameters" [S1]. In Figure 4 (right), the ResNet "converges to a lower training loss value but a similar test error" [S1].

Lower training loss with no gain at test time means the ResNet's extra capacity mostly goes into fitting the training set. The authors read this as DenseNets using parameters more efficiently, with a side effect that they are "less prone to overfitting" [S1].

The overfitting section gives further support. Without data augmentation, where overfitting is easiest, DenseNet's gains over prior work are largest [S1]:

- C10: error falls from 7.33% to 5.19%, a 29% relative reduction.
- C100: error falls from 28.20% to 19.64%, about 30%.

The authors saw possible overfitting in only one setting. On C10, raising $k$ from 12 to 24 gave 4× the parameters, yet error rose from 5.77% to 5.83% [S1]. They note that the bottleneck and compression layers "appear to be an effective way to counter this trend" [S1].

rejected.content:
It suggests the giant ResNet is partly **memorizing** its training images rather than learning patterns that carry over to new images, while the much smaller DenseNet-BC learns about as much useful knowledge with far less machinery.

Three ideas make this clearer. The first is general background, not something the paper defines. A network's **generalization gap** is the difference between how well it does on the images it practised on (training) and on fresh images it has never seen (test). It works like a student who memorizes the answer key: practice scores are perfect, exam scores are not. A big gap is called overfitting.

The second idea comes from the paper. In a DenseNet, each layer adds a small, fixed number of new "feature maps" (pattern detectors) for later layers to use. That number is the **growth rate**, written $k$. Raising $k$ from 12 to 24 makes the network about 4× larger [S1].

The third idea also comes from the paper. The "BC" in DenseNet-BC means two space-saving tricks. **Bottleneck** layers shrink what each layer has to process, and **compression** at the transition layers between blocks reduces how much is passed along. Together they make the network especially economical with its learnable numbers, called parameters [S1].

Now the comparison itself. DenseNet-BC with 100 layers and $k = 12$ gets 4.51% test error on C10+, against 4.62% for the 1001-layer ResNet. On C100+ the figures are 22.27% against 22.71%. The DenseNet uses 90% fewer parameters [S1]. The ResNet reaches a lower training loss but a similar test error [S1]. In other words, the ResNet fits its practice material more tightly, but that extra fit doesn't pay off on new images. Its generalization gap is bigger.

The authors read this as DenseNets using parameters more efficiently, which makes them less prone to overfitting [S1]. Further evidence appears on the harder versions of the datasets that use no data augmentation (the "+" means the training images were varied with shifts and flips). Without that help, overfitting is easier, and DenseNet's advantage grows. On C10, error drops from 7.33% to 5.19%, about a 29% relative reduction. On C100 it drops from 28.20% to 19.64%, about 30% [S1].

The authors saw possible overfitting in only one case. On C10, raising $k$ from 12 to 24 nudged error up from 5.77% to 5.83%. The bottleneck and compression layers appear to counter this [S1].

chosen.content:
No. Table 11 shows a strong overall scaling trend, but it is not monotone on every dataset [S1]. The extracted passage does not give the dataset names for the columns, so the columns below are identified by position (1 to 27).

**General trend.** Within each family, accuracy usually rises with scale [S1]:
- Column 1 goes from 81.1 (RN50) to 91.8 (RN50x64), and from 84.4 (B/32) to 93.8 (L/14-336px).
- Most other columns follow the same pattern, with RN50x64 and L/14 or L/14-336px at or near the top [S1].

**Where it breaks** [S1]:
- **Column 19** is the clearest reversal. RN50 scores 42.2, but RN101 drops to 33.3 and RN50x4 to 26.0. On the ViT side, B/16 reaches 44.0, while L/14 falls to 23.1 and L/14-336px to 21.9. The largest models are the worst here.
- **Column 24** is essentially flat and noisy, with every model between 17.0 and 28.1. RN50x4 (17.0) is below RN50 (20.3), and L/14 (24.3) does not beat B/32 (24.8).
- **Column 13**: RN101 (59.3) is below RN50 (66.6).
- **Column 16**: RN101 (33.1) and RN50x4 (35.0) are both below RN50 (41.1).
- **Column 21**: B/16 (48.1) is below B/32 (58.4).
- **Column 2**: there is a small regression from L/14 (96.2) to L/14-336px (95.7).

On the datasets that are hard or close to chance (columns 19 and 24 especially), scaling the backbone does not reliably help, and it can hurt.

rejected.content:
Making CLIP bigger usually helps, but not always. In the paper's full results table, a few datasets have larger models scoring the same or even worse than smaller ones [S1].

**Zero-shot classification** means the model sorts images into categories it was never specifically trained on. You give it the category names as text (like "a photo of a dog"), and it picks the description that best matches the image. The scores below measure how often it picks correctly, as a percentage, without any extra training on that dataset.

CLIP comes in two families of image-reading "engines." One is based on ResNet, an older, widely used design for processing images. The other is the **Vision Transformer** (ViT), which chops an image into small square patches and processes them somewhat like words in a sentence. In the table, the ResNet versions are named RN50 through RN50x64, and the ViT versions are B/32, B/16, L/14 and L/14-336px [S1].

Model scaling means making a model larger, with more internal parts and more computation, which usually lets it learn more. Within each family, the names roughly run from smaller to larger: RN50 up to RN50x64, and B/32 up to L/14-336px. The "336px" version also looks at higher-resolution images.

The table lists every model's zero-shot accuracy on 27 datasets [S1]. The passage gives the numbers but not the dataset names, so the columns below are identified by position:

- **The usual pattern:** in the first column, accuracy climbs fairly steadily with size, from 81.1 for RN50 to 93.8 for L/14-336px [S1]. Many columns behave like this.
- **Column 19, a clear reversal:** the smallest ResNet, RN50, scores 42.2, but the two largest ViT models score only 23.1 (L/14) and 21.9 (L/14-336px) [S1]. Even among ResNets, RN50x4 drops to 26.0 [S1].
- **Column 24, a bumpy pattern:** RN50 scores 20.3, RN101 rises to 28.1, then RN50x4 falls to 17.0 and RN50x16 to 17.6 before RN50x64 recovers to 27.5 [S1]. The biggest ViT only reaches 24.8 [S1].
- **Smaller dips elsewhere:** in column 21, B/16 scores 48.1, below the smaller B/32's 58.4 [S1]. In column 13, RN101 (59.3) is below RN50 (66.6) [S1].

The answer is no. Bigger is a strong general trend, but on some datasets it stalls or reverses. The table itself doesn't explain why. One plausible general reason is that some tasks are unusual or very specialized, so they don't benefit from the broad knowledge that larger models gain.

How exactly do they test Chinchilla for gender bias on Winogender? Like what does the model actually get scored on?
</question>

chosen.content:
The authors reuse the Winogender setup from Rae et al. (the Gopher paper) [S1]. Each input is a single sentence containing a pronoun that could refer to one of two occupational or participant roles. An example is "The librarian helped the child pick out a book because {pronoun} liked to encourage reading." [S1]

The probe is a zero-shot likelihood comparison. After the sentence, the model is given the continuation "'{Pronoun}' refers to the", and the authors measure the probability it assigns to completing it with each candidate role, here "librarian" vs. "child" [S1]. Each example is annotated with the correct resolution, which is the librarian in this case [S1]. So the model is scored on whether the role it ranks higher matches the gold annotation. In other words, this is a coreference accuracy metric read off the conditional probabilities. Nothing is generated.

The bias test comes from varying the pronoun. Every sentence is run three times, with a female, a male, and a gender-neutral pronoun [S1]. An unbiased model would pick the correct referent regardless of pronoun gender [S1]. Bias therefore shows up as accuracy that depends on the pronoun. For example, a model might resolve "he" to "librarian" less reliably than "she" because of occupational stereotypes.

This passage doesn't say how the per-pronoun accuracies are aggregated beyond that. For instance, it doesn't specify whether results are split into stereotype-consistent and stereotype-inconsistent subsets.

rejected.content:
Each test item gives Chinchilla a short sentence with a pronoun like "she" or "he," and the model is scored on whether it can tell which person that pronoun means. Then the same test is repeated with the pronoun swapped to see if the answer changes.

First, the skill being tested. When people read "The librarian helped the child pick out a book because she liked to encourage reading," they automatically know "she" means the librarian, not the child. Working out which person a word like "she" or "they" points back to is called **coreference resolution**. It is the skill this test measures [S1].

Second, how the model gets asked. A language model works by judging how likely each possible next word is, a bit like a very well-read autocomplete. So the authors don't ask Chinchilla a question directly. They give it the sentence, then add the start of a follow-up: "'She' refers to the …" They check how likely the model thinks "librarian" is as the next word compared with "child" [S1]. Whichever word the model rates as more likely counts as its answer.

Third, how this becomes a bias test. Each sentence has been labelled by people with the correct answer. In the example, the pronoun refers to the librarian [S1]. The key twist is that every sentence is run three times: once with a female pronoun, once with a male pronoun, and once with a gender-neutral one [S1]. So the model sees the "she" version, the "he" version, and the "they" version of the same sentence.

What the model is scored on, then, is whether it picks the correct person for each version. An unbiased model would get the right answer no matter which pronoun appears [S1]. If it gets "librarian" right with "she" but switches to "child" with "he," that suggests it is leaning on gender stereotypes about who librarians are rather than on what the sentence actually says.

The authors note they copied this setup from earlier work on the Gopher model, so the two can be compared fairly [S1].

Superficially, DenseNets are quite similar to ResNets: Eq. (2) differs from Eq. (1) only in that the inputs to H_l(·) are concatenated instead of summed. However, the implications of this seemingly small modification lead to substantially different behaviors of the two network architectures.

Model compactness. As a direct consequence of the input concatenation, the feature-maps learned by any of the DenseNet layers can be accessed by all subsequent layers. This encourages feature reuse throughout the network, and leads to more compact models.

The left two plots in Figure 4 show the result of an experiment that aims to compare the parameter efficiency of all variants of DenseNets (left) and also a comparable ResNet architecture (middle). We train multiple small networks with varying depths on C10+ and plot their test accuracies as a function of network parameters. In comparison with other popular network architectures, such as AlexNet [16] or VGG-net [29], ResNets with pre-activation use fewer parameters while typically achieving better results [12]. Hence, we compare DenseNet (k = 12) against this architecture. The training setting for DenseNet is kept the same as in the previous section.

The graph shows that DenseNet-BC is consistently the most parameter efficient variant of DenseNet. Further, to achieve the same level of accuracy, DenseNet-BC only requires around 1/3 of the parameters of ResNets (middle plot). This result is in line with the results on ImageNet we presented in Figure 3. The right plot in Figure 4 shows that a DenseNet-BC with only 0.8M trainable parameters is able to achieve comparable accuracy as the 1001-layer (pre-activation) ResNet [12] with 10.2M parameters.

Implicit Deep Supervision. One explanation for the improved accuracy of dense convolutional networks may be that individual layers receive additional supervision from the loss function through the shorter connections. One can interpret DenseNets to perform a kind of “deep supervision”. The benefits of deep supervision have previously been shown in deeply-supervised nets (DSN; [20]), which have classifiers attached to every hidden layer, enforcing the intermediate layers to learn discriminative features.
</source>
<source label="S2" section="§5 Discussion" pages="7-8">
DenseNets perform a similar deep supervision in an implicit fashion: a single classifier on top of the network provides direct supervision to all layers through at most two or three transition layers. However, the loss function and gradient of DenseNets are substantially less complicated, as the same loss function is shared between all layers.

Stochastic vs. deterministic connection. There is an interesting connection between dense convolutional networks and stochastic depth regularization of residual networks [13]. In stochastic depth, layers in residual networks are randomly dropped, which creates direct connections between the surrounding layers. As the pooling layers are never dropped, the network results in a similar connectivity pattern as DenseNet: there is a small probability for any two layers, between the same pooling layers, to be directly connected—if all intermediate layers are randomly dropped. Although the methods are ultimately quite different, the DenseNet interpretation of stochastic depth may provide insights into the success of this regularizer.

<question>
Why does swapping addition for concatenation make DenseNets need so many fewer parameters than ResNets for the same accuracy?
</question>

chosen.content:
The only formal change is in the layer input: ResNet computes $x_\ell = H_\ell(x_{\ell-1}) + x_{\ell-1}$, while DenseNet uses $x_\ell = H_\ell([x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{\ell-1}])$, concatenating rather than summing [S1]. The authors argue that this small change leads to substantially different behavior [S1].

Their explanation is accessibility. Because the inputs are concatenated, the feature-maps produced by any layer stay directly available to every later layer in the block. This encourages feature reuse and yields more compact models [S1]. A layer does not need to relearn or carry forward features that already exist. It only adds its $k$ new maps to the shared pool. A heat-map of average absolute weights from a trained $L=40$, $k=12$ network is the authors' check that later layers actually draw on earlier ones [S2].

As general background, not the paper's argument: in a residual sum, earlier features are mixed into a single fixed-width state. Preserving or isolating a specific feature then has to be handled implicitly by the weights at every subsequent width-$C$ layer. Concatenation keeps the features separate, so each layer can be narrow.

The evidence comes from C10+, where DenseNet-BC needs about 1/3 of the parameters of a pre-activation ResNet to reach the same accuracy [S1]. A 0.8M-parameter DenseNet-BC matches the 10.2M-parameter, 1001-layer pre-activation ResNet [S1]. On accuracy more broadly, the authors also suggest **implicit deep supervision**: the single classifier at the top supervises every layer directly through at most two or three transition layers, giving a shorter path to the loss [S1][S2].

rejected.content:
The paper calls this a "seemingly small modification": the only formal difference between the two designs is that each DenseNet layer **concatenates** the outputs of earlier layers, where a ResNet adds them together [S1]. That small change alters how information flows through the network [S1].

As general background (the paper takes ResNets as known), a ResNet's shortcut works like mixing paint. Each layer's output is added onto what came before, so the colours blend into one mixture. A later layer can't cleanly pull out "just the red from layer 3", because it has been stirred in with everything else. Concatenation is more like stacking labelled folders on a desk. Nothing is blended, and every earlier result stays separate and readable.

Because of this stacking, the features learned by any DenseNet layer (a **feature-map** is a layer's output, a grid recording where it spotted some pattern) "can be accessed by all subsequent layers" [S1]. This encourages feature reuse: a later layer that needs an edge detector built early on can read it directly instead of learning its own copy. Less relearning means fewer parameters, the adjustable numbers the network must learn, so the models are more compact [S1].

The authors tested this on C10+ (the CIFAR-10 image dataset with standard data augmentation). They trained small networks of different depths and compared accuracy against parameter count [S1]:

- To reach the same accuracy, DenseNet-BC needs only around 1/3 of the parameters of a pre-activation ResNet [S1].
- A DenseNet-BC with only 0.8M parameters matches the accuracy of a 1001-layer ResNet with 10.2M parameters [S1].

The authors also checked whether trained networks actually use this access. They measured how strongly each layer relies on each earlier layer's feature-maps and plotted the result as a heat-map [S2].

The next idea, deep supervision, is general background. "Supervision" is the feedback signal from the network's mistakes (the loss) that tells each layer how to improve. In a very deep network, that signal can grow weak by the time it travels back to the early layers. **Deep supervision** fixes this by giving inner layers their own direct feedback.

The authors suggest that DenseNets get a version of this for free, which may help explain their accuracy. The short connections let the single classifier at the top send feedback to every layer through at most two or three transition layers [S2]. Earlier deeply-supervised nets achieved something similar by attaching a classifier to every hidden layer [S1]. In DenseNets, all layers simply share one loss function [S2].

<question>
When they say CLIP got state of the art on 21 of 27 datasets in linear probes, does that mean it had the single highest score, or something looser?
</question>

chosen.content:
Something looser. "State of the art" here means CLIP ViT-L/14@336px scored inside the Clopper-Pearson 99.5% confidence interval around each dataset's top score [S1]. So on some of those 21 datasets another model may have the single highest number, and CLIP still counts because its score is statistically indistinguishable from it at that confidence level.

You can see this in the raw rows. On CIFAR-10, for example, L/14 at 224px has 98.0 and L/14-336px has 97.9 [S2]. A strict "highest score" criterion would not credit the 336px model there, but the interval criterion does.

The protocol is the standard **linear probe**: the pre-trained encoder is frozen, and a linear classifier is trained on its features for each of the 27 datasets [S1]. It measures how linearly separable the representation is, not how well the full network performs after fine-tuning.

In Table 10, the scores that fall inside each dataset's 99.5% interval are shown in bold [S1]. A dataset can therefore have several bolded entries, and the "21 of 27" counts the datasets where the best CLIP model is among them.

The authors also point out that on many datasets CLIP's margin is large, not just a tie within the interval. They read this as evidence that natural language supervision beats traditional pre-training based on image classification [S1].

The paper doesn't spell out how the Clopper-Pearson interval is computed for metrics that aren't simple proportions, such as 11-point mAP, mean-per-class accuracy, or ROC AUC. The interval is naturally defined for binomial accuracy, so for those metrics the "within CI" call is presumably an approximation.

rejected.content:
It's something looser. "State of the art" here means CLIP's score was **statistically indistinguishable** from the top score on that dataset, not necessarily the single highest number [S1]. Three ideas explain what that means.

**Linear probe evaluation.** This is how the paper tests what CLIP has learned. The trained model is "frozen," meaning no further changes are made to it. It turns each image into a list of numbers that summarizes what it sees. Then a very simple classifier, essentially a straight-line rule, is trained on top of those numbers to sort images into categories. If even this simple rule works well, the frozen model must have learned useful descriptions of images. The paper compares many pre-trained models this way across 27 datasets [S1].

**Confidence interval.** This is general background, not something the paper explains. A test set is a sample of images, so every score contains some luck. A slightly different set of test images might have shifted it up or down a little. A confidence interval is a range around a score that says "the true value is very likely somewhere in here." Think of two runners whose times differ by a hundredth of a second, when the stopwatch is only accurate to a tenth. Calling one of them faster isn't justified.

**Clopper-Pearson interval.** This is also general background. It is one specific, cautious way to compute that range when the score counts right-versus-wrong answers, such as accuracy. "99.5%" means the range is built to be very wide and safe, so a score has to fall well below it to count as clearly worse.

Now the paper's rule. For each dataset, the authors took the top score from any model and drew a 99.5% Clopper-Pearson interval around it. The best CLIP model counted as state of the art if its score landed inside that interval [S1]. That model uses the ViT-L/14 design and looks at images at 336 by 336 pixels. It met this bar on 21 of the 27 datasets [S1]. Scores falling inside the interval are shown in bold in Table 10, so a dataset can have more than one bold entry [S1].

So on some of those 21 datasets, another model may have scored a bit higher, but the gap was too small to call meaningful. The authors also point out that on many datasets CLIP wins by a large margin, not just a tie [S1]. They read this as evidence that learning from natural-language captions works better than the traditional approach of pre-training on labelled image categories [S1].

<question>
Why does Wikipedia get repeated over 3 times during training while News and GitHub aren't even fully seen once?
</question>

chosen.content:
The number of epochs for a subset is set by how much of the training budget is assigned to it compared with how much data it contains. A small subset with a meaningful share has to be repeated. A large subset with a modest share runs out of training before its data does.

Three pieces of general background are needed first:

1. **Epoch**: one full pass over a dataset. Here it is counted per subset, so "3.40 epochs" means the average Wikipedia token is seen about 3.4 times.
2. **Sampling proportions**: training batches are drawn from each subset at a fixed rate, independent of the subset's size. The mixture fixes what fraction of all training tokens comes from each source.
3. **Tokens vs. disk size**: the budget is counted in tokens, while disk size only roughly tracks token count. Compression and the tokenizer affect the ratio, so disk size indicates scale but cannot be converted exactly.

In the paper, training runs for 1.4 trillion tokens, and each MassiveText subset has a fixed sampling proportion [S1]. The subsets compare as follows:

- **Wikipedia** is tiny at 0.001 TB but is sampled at 1% [S1]. Since 1% of 1.4T is 14B tokens, far more than the subset holds, it gets cycled 3.40 times [S1].
- **News** at 2.7 TB and **GitHub** at 3.1 TB are the largest subsets but are sampled at only 10% and 4% [S1]. They reach just 0.21 and 0.13 epochs [S1], so most of their data is never used.
- **MassiveWeb** also goes past one pass. It is 1.9 TB and sampled at 45%, giving 1.24 epochs [S1]. The authors note that both MassiveWeb and Wikipedia are used for more than one epoch [S1].

The mixture is a slight reweighting of the one in Rae et al. (2021) [S1]. Books rose from 27% to 30%, Wikipedia fell from 2% to 1%, MassiveWeb fell from 48% to 45%, and GitHub rose from 3% to 4% [S1]. The paper doesn't explain why these proportions were chosen, or why repeating Wikipedia was preferred to drawing more from News or GitHub. It simply reports the mixture and the epoch counts that result.

rejected.content:
The number of repeats isn't chosen directly. It falls out of two things: how big each data source is, and what share of the training text the authors decided to draw from it [S1].

**Three ideas first**

An **epoch** means one complete pass through a dataset. If you read a book cover to cover once, that's one epoch. Reading it three and a half times is 3.4 epochs. Reading only a fifth of it is 0.2 epochs.

Chinchilla's training data is a mix of several sources: web pages, books, news, code from GitHub, Wikipedia, and others. Each source has a **sampling proportion**, the share of the total training text that comes from it [S1]. Think of a recipe that says "45% flour, 30% sugar, 1% salt": the recipe fixes the shares regardless of how much of each ingredient is in the pantry.

The paper measures how much training happens in **tokens**, small chunks of text roughly the size of a word or part of a word. Chinchilla is trained on 1.4 trillion of them [S1]. The table lists each source's size on disk in terabytes [S1]. That isn't a token count, but a bigger disk size generally means more text.

**Putting it together**

Wikipedia is tiny: just 0.001 TB on disk. Yet it supplies 1% of the 1.4 trillion training tokens [S1]. That 1% is far more text than Wikipedia actually contains, so the model cycles through it about 3.40 times [S1]. It's like using a whole pantry jar of salt three times over because the recipe is huge.

News and GitHub are the opposite case. They are among the largest sources, at 2.7 TB and 3.1 TB, but they get only 10% and 4% of the budget [S1]. That share isn't enough to get through them even once, so the model sees about 0.21 of News and 0.13 of GitHub [S1].

Wikipedia isn't the only source that repeats. MassiveWeb, the web-page collection, is also used for more than one epoch, at 1.24 [S1].

**A small change from earlier work**

These shares differ slightly from those in an earlier DeepMind paper by Rae et al. (2021) [S1]. Books went up from 27% to 30%, Wikipedia went down from 2% to 1%, MassiveWeb went down from 48% to 45%, and GitHub went up from 3% to 4% [S1]. The paper doesn't say why the authors chose these particular shares or why they adjusted them.

<question>
Why do they fit a parabola to each fixed-compute curve, and how does that get them to the a=0.49 / b=0.51 exponents?
</question>

chosen.content:
The parabola finds the best model size for each compute budget. The exponents then describe how that best size moves as the budget grows. Three ideas make this easier to follow.

**Background (not from the paper).** A **scaling law** is a simple rule of the form "if you multiply one thing by some factor, another thing changes by a predictable factor." Here the question is how big a model should be, and how much text it should read, as you spend more computing power.

**Compute.** The paper measures computing power in FLOPs, a count of basic arithmetic operations. It uses the approximation that training costs about 6 × (number of parameters) × (number of training tokens) [S2]. Parameters are the model's adjustable numbers, a rough measure of its size. Tokens are word-pieces of training text. With the budget fixed, a bigger model must read fewer tokens, and a smaller one gets more [S1].

**Background (not from the paper).** A **learning rate schedule** controls how big the model's adjustment steps are during training. A cosine schedule starts with large steps and smoothly shrinks them toward the end. The authors set the schedule's length to match the number of tokens each model trains on [S1]. That way every model gets a properly finished training run and the comparison is fair.

**Why a parabola.** The authors picked 9 compute budgets, from 6 × 10^18 to 3 × 10^21 FLOPs [S1]. For each budget, they trained models of many sizes and recorded each model's final loss, which measures how wrong its predictions are (lower is better) [S1]. Plotting loss against model size gives a valley [S1]:

- Too small a model can't learn enough, even with lots of text.
- Too big a model runs out of budget before it has read enough text.

The best size sits at the bottom of the valley. Each measured point is a little noisy, so instead of picking the single lowest point, they fit a parabola (a smooth U-shaped curve) through the points and read off where its bottom is [S1]. This gives one "best model size" per budget. The matching token count then follows from the compute formula [S1].

**From 9 bottoms to the exponents.** They now have 9 pairs of (budget, best size) and (budget, best token count). They fit a scaling-law curve through these pairs, one rule for the best size and one for the best token count as the budget grows [S1]. The exponent says how fast each one grows: the best size grows like the budget raised to the power a, and the best token count like the budget raised to b. The fit gives a = 0.49 and b = 0.51 [S1].

Both numbers are close to one half, and they add up to about 1. So when compute grows, it should be split roughly evenly between a bigger model and more training text. If you get 4× more compute, you make the model about 2× bigger and train it on about 2× more tokens. The paper's third approach, using a different method, lands nearby at a = 0.46 and b = 0.54 [S2].

rejected.content:
Each IsoFLOP run fixes total training compute, so at a given budget, choosing $N$ determines $D$ (footnote 6) [S1]. The authors train models of different sizes at each of 9 budgets, from $6\times10^{18}$ to $3\times10^{21}$ FLOPs, and record only the final smoothed loss. Approach 1 instead used $(N, D, L)$ points along entire training runs [S1]. Each budget's loss-versus-$N$ curve shows a clear valley, and they sampled enough model sizes to make sure the minimum is visible [S1].

The parabola is a local model of that valley. Fitting it to each IsoFLOP curve lets them estimate the model size at which the minimum loss is reached directly, not just pick the best of the discrete sizes they trained [S1]. That gives one estimate $N_{opt}(C)$ per budget, and $D_{opt}(C)$ follows from the compute constraint.

The paper doesn't say what parametrization the parabola uses. In general, such fits are done in $\log N$, where the valley is roughly symmetric.

The second stage is a power-law regression across the 9 budgets, $N_{opt}\propto C^a$ and $D_{opt}\propto C^b$, which gives $a=0.49$ and $b=0.51$ [S1]. Approach 3 uses $C\approx 6ND$ [S2]. Under that relation, $a+b$ must be about 1, so the result amounts to splitting compute almost equally between parameters and tokens.

A fairness detail: the cosine schedule length is set to match each run's token count, which Appendix B finds optimal [S1]. Without this, smaller models trained on more tokens would be compared against a mismatched schedule, which would bias where the valley sits.

We proposed a new convolutional network architecture, which we refer to as Dense Convolutional Network (DenseNet). It introduces direct connections between any two layers with the same feature-map size. We showed that DenseNets scale naturally to hundreds of layers, while exhibiting no optimization difficulties.
