**Retrieval-augmented language models.** As general background, these models work like a student allowed to look things up during an exam. Before writing each part of its output, the model searches a large library of text and reads relevant passages. The paper names this approach and points to work by Borgeaud et al. (2021) and others as examples [S1].

**Mixture of experts (MoE).** Also as background, an MoE model is like a large company with many specialist departments, where each task goes to only a few of them. The model can have an enormous number of parameters (its adjustable internal settings, roughly its "size"), but only a small part of it works on any one piece of text. That keeps it cheap to run.

**Training tokens.** In general, a token is a small chunk of text, about a word or part of a word. The number of training tokens is the amount of text a model reads while it learns.

The paper's argument is this: adding retrieval "effectively increases the number of data tokens seen during training," by a factor of about 10 in Borgeaud et al.'s case [S1]. The looked-up passages work like extra reading material, so a model with retrieval learns from far more text than its own training set alone. Retrieval models do very well even without being huge. From this, the authors conclude that "the performance of language models may be more dependant on the size of the training data than previously thought" [S1].

This matters for the paper's main claim. The authors argue that model size and the amount of training text should grow together, and they note that this is "in clear contrast to previous work" [S2]. Retrieval is outside evidence that fits their view: give a model more data, and it improves a lot.

MoE models make a useful contrast because they push in the other direction. They grow the model's effective size while keeping computing cost fairly low, but the paper notes that these savings "seem to diminish" for very large models [S1]. Making a model bigger has limits. Giving it more data, as retrieval effectively does, appears to be an underused way to improve it.

rejected.content:
Retrieval-augmented transformers condition each prediction on text fetched from an external corpus, so during training the model is exposed to far more token content than the nominal training set alone. The authors frame this as effectively increasing the number of data tokens seen during training, by a factor of ~10 in Borgeaud et al. (2021), the RETRO paper [S1].

The inference is indirect. If a retrieval model gets large gains mainly by seeing more tokens, not by adding much capacity, then data volume is a stronger lever on loss than the parameter-centric view assumed. The authors conclude that language-model performance "may be more dependant on the size of the training data than previously thought" [S1]. This anticipates their main result: under a fixed FLOP budget, parameter count and training tokens should be scaled equally. They describe this as a clear contrast to previous work [S2].

The placement next to MoE is deliberate. Routed models such as the 1.7T-parameter Switch transformer and 1.2T-parameter GLaM increase *effective model size* while using relatively fewer training and inference FLOPs [S1]. However, these computational benefits seem to diminish for very large models [S1]. The authors present retrieval as an orthogonal approach [S1]. MoE scales the parameter axis cheaply, with fading returns at scale, while retrieval scales the data axis and still pays off. That asymmetry supports their argument that existing large dense models are under-trained on data relative to their size.

chosen.content:
A **scaling law** is a fitted power-law relationship that predicts a model's final loss from its size $N$ (parameters) and its training data $D$ (tokens). Researchers fit it on small runs and extrapolate it to large ones. **Compute-optimal training** asks how to split a fixed compute budget between $N$ and $D$ so that the loss is as low as possible. That budget is measured in FLOPs, the total number of floating-point operations used in training. As general background, training compute is commonly estimated as $C \approx 6ND$, so at a fixed $N$, extra tokens mean proportionally extra FLOPs.

Table A3 gives, for each model size, the compute-optimal token count and FLOPs predicted by Approach 2 (IsoFLOP profiles) and Approach 3 (the parametric loss fit) [S1]. Approach 3 recommends more tokens at every size, and the gap grows steadily with scale [S1]:

| Parameters | Approach 2 tokens | Approach 3 tokens | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 400M | 7.7B | 9.2B | ~1.2× |
| 1B | 20.0B | 27.1B | ~1.4× |
| 10B | 219.5B | 410.1B | ~1.9× |
| 67B | 1.7T | 4.1T | ~2.4× |
| 280B | 7.1T | 20.1T | ~2.8× |
| 1T | 26.5T | 94.1T | ~3.6× |
| 10T | 292.0T | 1425.5T | ~4.9× |

The ratios are computed here from the table's values. The FLOPs columns follow the same pattern. At 10T parameters, for example, Approach 3 calls for 8.55e+28 FLOPs against 1.75e+28 for Approach 2 [S1].

One row looks wrong. For 175B parameters, Approach 3 lists 12.0T tokens but only 1.26e+24 FLOPs [S1]. That is less than its own 67B entry of 1.71e+24 [S1], even though the 175B model is larger and trains on more tokens. As general background, $6 \times 175\text{B} \times 12.0\text{T} \approx 1.26\text{e+}25$, so the exponent is most likely a typo and should be 25, not 24. The paper itself doesn't comment on this.

In general terms, a widening ratio is what you would expect when two methods fit slightly different exponents for how data should scale with compute. A small difference in slope on a log-log plot compounds over many orders of magnitude. Figure A3 shows this directly: it plots the predicted optimal tokens and parameters against FLOP budget for all three approaches, so you can see the frontiers spread apart as the budget grows [S1].

rejected.content:
Approach 3 always recommends more training text than Approach 2 for the same model size, and the gap grows steadily as models get bigger: from about 1.2 times as many tokens for small models to about 5 times as many for the largest ones in the table.

Three ideas from general background (not from the passages shown here) make the comparison easier to read:

- **Scaling laws** are rules of thumb that predict how good a language model will get as it grows bigger or reads more text. They work like a growth chart that lets you guess an adult's height from a child's.
- **Compute-optimal training** asks a budget question: with a fixed amount of computer work, how should you split it between a bigger model and more reading material to get the best result? Approaches 2 and 3 are two different ways of answering it.
- **FLOPs** count the basic arithmetic steps a computer does, so they measure how much computing a training run costs. A number like "1.2e+20" means 1.2 followed by 20 zeros.

Table A3 lists, for each model size, how many tokens (pieces of text, roughly word fragments) and FLOPs each approach recommends [S1]. Here are a few rows:

| Model size | Approach 2 tokens | Approach 3 tokens | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 400 Million | 7.7 Billion | 9.2 Billion | ~1.2× |
| 1 Billion | 20.0 Billion | 27.1 Billion | ~1.4× |
| 10 Billion | 219.5 Billion | 410.1 Billion | ~1.9× |
| 67 Billion | 1.7 Trillion | 4.1 Trillion | ~2.4× |
| 1 Trillion | 26.5 Trillion | 94.1 Trillion | ~3.6× |
| 10 Trillion | 292.0 Trillion | 1425.5 Trillion | ~4.9× |

(numbers from [S1]; ratios computed from them)

So yes, the gap widens with scale. For small models the two methods nearly agree. For a 10-trillion-parameter model, Approach 3 asks for close to five times as much text [S1]. Because more text means more computing, Approach 3's FLOP estimates are also higher in nearly every row. At 10 Trillion parameters, for example, it gives 8.55e+28 against 1.75e+28 for Approach 2 [S1].

One row looks wrong. At 175 Billion parameters, Approach 3 lists 1.26e+24 FLOPs. That is less than its own 67 Billion entry of 1.71e+24 and less than Approach 2's 4.54e+24 for the same size, even though Approach 3 recommends far more tokens there (12.0 Trillion vs 4.3 Trillion) [S1]. A bigger model reading more text cannot cost less, so this figure is most likely a typo. The token count in that row fits the trend.

To see the same pattern as a picture, Figure A3 plots the recommended model size and token count against the FLOP budget for all three approaches, Approach 1 included [S1]. The lines there spread apart in the same way as the budget grows.

Why does Wikipedia get repeated over 3 times during training while News and GitHub aren't even fully seen once?

chosen.content:
The number of repeats isn't chosen directly. It falls out of two things: how big each data source is, and what share of the training text the authors decided to draw from it [S1].

**Three ideas first**

An **epoch** means one complete pass through a dataset. If you read a book cover to cover once, that's one epoch. Reading it three and a half times is 3.4 epochs. Reading only a fifth of it is 0.2 epochs.

Chinchilla's training data is a mix of several sources: web pages, books, news, code from GitHub, Wikipedia, and others. Each source has a **sampling proportion**, the share of the total training text that comes from it [S1]. Think of a recipe that says "45% flour, 30% sugar, 1% salt": the recipe fixes the shares regardless of how much of each ingredient is in the pantry.

The paper measures how much training happens in **tokens**, small chunks of text roughly the size of a word or part of a word. Chinchilla is trained on 1.4 trillion of them [S1]. The table lists each source's size on disk in terabytes [S1]. That isn't a token count, but a bigger disk size generally means more text.

**Putting it together**

Wikipedia is tiny: just 0.001 TB on disk. Yet it supplies 1% of the 1.4 trillion training tokens [S1]. That 1% is far more text than Wikipedia actually contains, so the model cycles through it about 3.40 times [S1]. It's like using a whole pantry jar of salt three times over because the recipe is huge.

News and GitHub are the opposite case. They are among the largest sources, at 2.7 TB and 3.1 TB, but they get only 10% and 4% of the budget [S1]. That share isn't enough to get through them even once, so the model sees about 0.21 of News and 0.13 of GitHub [S1].

Wikipedia isn't the only source that repeats. MassiveWeb, the web-page collection, is also used for more than one epoch, at 1.24 [S1].

**A small change from earlier work**

These shares differ slightly from those in an earlier DeepMind paper by Rae et al. (2021) [S1]. Books went up from 27% to 30%, Wikipedia went down from 2% to 1%, MassiveWeb went down from 48% to 45%, and GitHub went up from 3% to 4% [S1]. The paper doesn't say why the authors chose these particular shares or why they adjusted them.

rejected.content:
The epoch count isn't chosen directly. It falls out of the sampling proportion: each subset's share of the 1.4T-token budget divided by the subset's size [S1].

- **Wikipedia** is tiny (0.001 TB, 6M documents) but is sampled at 1%. Its ~14B-token allotment exceeds its contents, so it gets cycled 3.40 times [S1].
- **News** (2.7 TB) and **GitHub** (3.1 TB) are the largest subsets on disk, but are sampled at only 10% and 4%. That gives 0.21 and 0.13 epochs, so most of their data is never seen [S1].
- **MassiveWeb** also exceeds one epoch (1.24), since it gets 45% of the mixture from 1.9 TB [S1]. The authors explicitly flag both MassiveWeb and Wikipedia as being used for more than one epoch [S1].

The mixture is a slight reweighting of the one in Rae et al. (2021) [S1]:

- MassiveWeb goes from 48% to 45%.
- Books goes from 27% to 30%.
- GitHub goes from 3% to 4%.
- Wikipedia goes from 2% to 1%.
- C4 and News stay at 10% [S1].

The paper doesn't explain why these proportions were chosen, or why Wikipedia was halved.

As general background rather than the paper's claim: mixture weights in LM pretraining usually reflect a judgment about per-source quality and usefulness, not raw availability. Small, curated sources like Wikipedia are commonly upsampled past one epoch, and large, noisier or narrower sources are subsampled. A few repeats of a small corpus are generally considered low-risk for overfitting at this scale.

chosen.content:
Mostly yes, but not always. Across the 27 datasets in Table 11, larger CLIP models usually score higher, but several columns break the trend [S1].

Three terms help in reading the table. The cited passage is only the table, so these definitions are general background, not text from the passage.

- **Zero-shot classification** means CLIP is not trained on the target dataset. Each class name is turned into a text prompt and embedded. The image is assigned to the class whose text embedding has the highest cosine similarity with the image embedding.
- A Vision Transformer (ViT) splits an image into patches and processes them as a sequence of tokens. "B/32" means a Base-size model with 32×32-pixel patches, and "L/14" means a Large model with 14×14 patches. Smaller patches give more tokens and more compute.
- Model scaling increases width, depth and input resolution together. RN50x4, x16 and x64 are ResNet-50s scaled to roughly that multiple of compute. "336px" means the model runs on higher-resolution inputs.

The table lists nine backbones: RN50, RN101, RN50x4, RN50x16 and RN50x64, then ViT B/32, B/16, L/14 and L/14-336px [S1]. The general trend is clear in the first column, which rises from 81.1 for RN50 to 93.8 for L/14-336px [S1]. The passage doesn't say which dataset each column is, so the columns below are counted by position from the left.

Clear exceptions:

- **Column 19:** RN50 scores 42.2 and B/16 scores 44.0. The largest ViTs drop to 23.1 (L/14) and 21.9 (L/14-336px), and RN50x4 falls to 26.0 [S1]. The biggest models are roughly half as accurate as the smallest one here.
- **Column 24:** RN50 scores 20.3 and RN101 scores 28.1. RN50x4 then drops to 17.0 and RN50x16 to 17.6, and no ViT goes above 24.8 [S1]. The scores move up and down with no consistent pattern.
- **Column 21:** B/16 scores 48.1, well below B/32 at 58.4 [S1].
- **Columns 13 and 16:** RN101 scores below RN50, with 59.3 vs 66.6 and 33.1 vs 41.1 [S1].
- **Column 2:** L/14-336px scores slightly below L/14, at 95.7 vs 96.2 [S1].

Most of these columns have low absolute accuracy. That suggests tasks where zero-shot CLIP is weak overall, so scores may be noisy or near chance. On those tasks, extra capacity does not reliably help. The general background on how zero-shot prompts work suggests prompt or label mismatch as one plausible cause, but the cited passage does not explain the drops.

No. Table 11 shows a strong overall scaling trend, but it is not monotone on every dataset [S1]. The extracted passage does not give the dataset names for the columns, so the columns below are identified by position (1 to 27).

- Column 1 goes from 81.1 (RN50) to 91.8 (RN50x64), and from 84.4 (B/32) to 93.8 (L/14-336px).
- Most other columns follow the same pattern, with RN50x64 and L/14 or L/14-336px at or near the top [S1].

**Where it breaks** [S1]:
- **Column 19** is the clearest reversal. RN50 scores 42.2, but RN101 drops to 33.3 and RN50x4 to 26.0. On the ViT side, B/16 reaches 44.0, while L/14 falls to 23.1 and L/14-336px to 21.9. The largest models are the worst here.
- **Column 24** is essentially flat and noisy, with every model between 17.0 and 28.1. RN50x4 (17.0) is below RN50 (20.3), and L/14 (24.3) does not beat B/32 (24.8).

- **Column 16**: RN101 (33.1) and RN50x4 (35.0) are both below RN50 (41.1).

- **Column 2**: there is a small regression from L/14 (96.2) to L/14-336px (95.7).

chosen.content:
The authors call current LLMs oversized because their fitted scaling exponents imply that parameters and tokens should grow at the same rate with compute. Writing $N_{opt} \propto C^a$ and $D_{opt} \propto C^b$, all three estimation methods give $a \approx b \approx 0.5$: 0.50/0.50 from training-curve minima, 0.49/0.51 from IsoFLOP profiles, and 0.46/0.54 from the parametric loss fit [S1]. This contrasts with Kaplan et al.'s 0.73/0.27, which puts most of the extra compute into model size [S1]. Under the equal-scaling rule, models sized by the Kaplan-style allocation have too many parameters and too few tokens for the compute they used.

For a 175B model, the text says the compute-optimal setup is $4.41 \times 10^{24}$ FLOPs and over 4.2 trillion tokens [S1]. Table 3, which uses the Approach 1 projections, gives somewhat lower figures for the same size: $3.85 \times 10^{24}$ FLOPs and 3.7 trillion tokens [S2]. Either way, that is far more data than current large models are trained on [S1]. The flip side is that at GPT-3-scale budgets, a smaller model trained on more tokens would reach lower loss [S1]. By the same rule, a 1T-parameter model only becomes optimal at about $10^{26}$ FLOPs [S1].

There are two caveats. The authors acknowledge significant uncertainty when extrapolating across many orders of magnitude [S1]. They also reproduce the IsoFLOP analysis on C4 and GitHub code and reach the same equal-proportion conclusion, which supports the claim that it holds beyond their main training dataset [S1].

rejected.content:
A few ideas come first, because the claim rests on them.

A **scaling law** is a rule of thumb that predicts how much better a language model gets as you make it bigger or train it longer. It works like a recipe that tells you how to scale up the ingredients. The authors use scaling laws to answer one question: if you have a fixed amount of computing to spend, how should you split it?

That fixed amount of computing is measured in **training FLOPs**, a count of the basic arithmetic operations (additions and multiplications) the computers perform during training. Think of it as your total budget. You can spend it on a bigger model (more "parameters", the adjustable numbers inside the model) or on showing the model more text (more "tokens", roughly word-pieces).

The authors' main method, an **IsoFLOP analysis**, holds the budget fixed and trains many models of different sizes with it. The small ones see lots of text and the big ones see less. Whichever ends up best shows the right split for that budget. Repeating this at several budgets reveals the trend.

Here is what they found. As the budget grows, model size and the amount of training text should grow by the same proportion: if one doubles, the other should double too [S1]. Three separate methods all point to this near-equal split [S1]. An earlier study by Kaplan et al. had concluded that most extra budget should go into making the model bigger, with only a small share going to more data [S1]. Models like GPT-3 were built along those lines: very large, but trained on comparatively little text.

That is why the authors call such models "considerably over-sized, given their respective compute budgets" [S1]. For a 175-billion-parameter model like GPT-3, they estimate it should be trained with a budget of $4.41 \times 10^{24}$ FLOPs (4.41 followed by 24 zeros) and on over 4.2 trillion tokens [S1]. That is far more data than large models were trained on at the time [S1]. A table in the same section, based on one of the three methods, gives a slightly lower estimate for 175 billion parameters: 3.7 trillion tokens [S2]. Either way, the answer is trillions of tokens.

The practical upshot is that, with the budgets already used, smaller models trained on more text would have performed better [S1]. The authors admit there is "significant uncertainty" when predicting this far beyond the models they actually trained [S1]. Still, they repeated the analysis on two other kinds of text, the C4 web dataset and GitHub code, and reached the same equal-scaling conclusion [S1].

<source label="S1" section="§1 Introduction" pages="1">
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become the dominant machine learning approach for visual object recognition. Although they were originally introduced over 20 years ago [18], improvements in computer hardware and network structure have enabled the training of truly deep CNNs only recently. The original LeNet5 [19] consisted of 5 layers, VGG featured 19 [29], and only last year Highway Networks [34] and Residual Networks (ResNets) [11] have surpassed the 100-layer barrier.

As CNNs become increasingly deep, a new research problem emerges: as information about the input or gradient passes through many layers, it can vanish and “wash out” by the time it reaches the end (or beginning) of the network. Many recent publications address this or related problems. ResNets [11] and Highway Networks [34] bypass signal from one layer to the next via identity connections. Stochastic depth [13] shortens ResNets by randomly dropping layers during training to allow better information and gradient flow. FractalNets [17] repeatedly combine several parallel layer sequences with different number of convolutional blocks to obtain a large nominal depth, while maintaining many short paths in the network. Although these different approaches vary in network topology and training procedure, they all share a key characteristic: they create short paths from early layers to later layers.
</source>
<source label="S2" section="§1 Introduction" pages="2">
In this paper, we propose an architecture that distills this insight into a simple connectivity pattern: to ensure maximum information flow between layers in the network, we connect all layers (with matching feature-map sizes) directly with each other. To preserve the feed-forward nature, each layer obtains additional inputs from all preceding layers and passes on its own feature-maps to all subsequent layers. Figure 1 illustrates this layout schematically. Crucially, in contrast to ResNets, we never combine features through summation before they are passed into a layer; instead, we combine features by concatenating them. Hence, the l^th layer has linputs, consisting of the feature-maps of all preceding convolutional blocks. Its own feature-maps are passed on to all L−lsubsequent layers. This introduces ^{L(L+1)} connections in an L-layer network, instead of just 2 L, as in traditional architectures. Because of its dense connectivity pattern, we refer to our approach as Dense Convolutional Network (DenseNet).

A possibly counter-intuitive effect of this dense connectivity pattern is that it requires fewer parameters than traditional convolutional networks, as there is no need to relearn redundant feature-maps. Traditional feed-forward architectures can be viewed as algorithms with a state, which is passed on from layer to layer. Each layer reads the state from its preceding layer and writes to the subsequent layer. It changes the state but also passes on information that needs to be preserved. ResNets [11] make this information preservation explicit through additive identity transformations. Recent variations of ResNets [13] show that many layers contribute very little and can in fact be randomly dropped during training. This makes the state of ResNets similar to (unrolled) recurrent neural networks [21], but the number of parameters of ResNets is substantially larger because each layer has its own weights. Our proposed DenseNet architecture explicitly differentiates between information that is added to the network and information that is preserved. DenseNet layers are very narrow (e.g., 12 filters per layer), adding only a small set of feature-maps to the “collective knowledge” of the network and keep the remaining feature-maps unchanged—and the final classifier makes a decision based on all feature-maps in the network.
</source>
</sources>

<question>
What's the common thread between ResNets, Highway Networks, stochastic depth, and FractalNets? They seem like pretty different designs.
</question>

chosen.content:
The common thread is that all four designs create **short paths** from early layers to later ones [S1]. Their shapes and training tricks differ, but each gives information a shortcut instead of forcing it through every layer in turn [S1].

That matters because of the problem they all target. As networks got very deep (past 100 layers in recent designs), information about the input, or the training signal coming back from the output, can fade and "wash out" by the time it has crossed many layers [S1].

Three background ideas explain why that fading happens and how a shortcut helps. The paper assumes them, so the definitions here are general background rather than the paper's own content:

1. **Vanishing gradient problem.** A network learns from a correction signal that says how each layer should adjust. In a very deep network this signal can shrink a little at every layer until it is too faint to teach the early layers anything. This is the fading the four methods fight.
2. **Residual connections.** A residual connection is a bypass that lets a layer's input skip around it and rejoin on the other side unchanged. It is like an express lane next to a road with many traffic lights, so the signal can arrive without passing every light. This is the core trick of ResNets.
3. **Backpropagation.** This is the step-by-step way the correction signal travels backward from the output toward the input. Because it passes through layers one after another, a long chain weakens it, and a bypass gives it a shorter route.

With those ideas in place, here is how each method builds its shortcuts:

- **ResNets and Highway Networks** pass the signal from one layer to the next through "identity connections," which are bypasses that carry it across unchanged [S1].
- **Stochastic depth** randomly drops layers during training. This makes the network effectively shorter at each step, which helps information and the training signal flow [S1].
- **FractalNets** combine several parallel chains of layers that have different lengths. The network is very deep on paper, but it still has many short routes through it [S1].

The authors build DenseNet directly on this shared insight. Instead of adding a few shortcuts, DenseNet connects every layer directly to every later layer (among layers whose outputs have the same size), aiming for "maximum information flow" [S2]. One difference from ResNets is that DenseNet does not add the incoming information together. It stacks the earlier layers' outputs side by side, so each layer sees the outputs of all the layers before it [S2].

rejected.content:
They all target the same failure mode of very deep CNNs. As input information moves forward, or gradients move backward, through many layers, the signal can vanish and "wash out" before it reaches the other end of the network [S1]. Each design is a different way around that depth bottleneck:

- **ResNets and Highway Networks** pass the signal from one layer to the next through identity connections. The identity path carries information that the stacked transformation would otherwise have to preserve on its own [S1].
- **Stochastic depth** randomly drops layers of a ResNet during training. This shortens the effective network on each pass and improves information and gradient flow [S1]. The authors also note it shows that many ResNet layers contribute very little [S2].
- **FractalNets** repeatedly combine parallel layer sequences that have different numbers of convolutional blocks. This gives a large nominal depth while keeping many short paths through the network [S1].

The topologies and training procedures differ, but the authors point out that all four share one property: they create short paths from early layers to later layers [S1].

DenseNet takes this observation to its extreme. It connects every layer directly to every subsequent layer that has the same feature-map size, so the shortest path between any two layers is a single connection [S2]. The main structural difference from ResNets is how features are merged. ResNets add features, while DenseNet concatenates them before they enter a layer. As a result, earlier feature-maps are carried forward unchanged rather than mixed into a running state, and each layer adds only a small set of new maps, for example 12 filters per layer [S2].

<question>
Why does CLIP scale the image encoder along width, depth and resolution together but only make the text encoder wider?

chosen.content:
A CNN can be scaled along three axes, and the paper scales the image encoder along all three because earlier work found that this uses compute better than scaling one axis. The text encoder gets only width because the authors found CLIP's performance depends less on its capacity.

The paper uses these terms without defining them. In general:

- **Width** is the number of channels or hidden units per layer, so each layer computes richer features.
- **Depth** is the number of layers, so the network composes more stages of processing.
- **Resolution** is the pixel size of the input image, so the network sees finer detail. It costs compute because every convolutional feature map grows with the input.
- **Compound scaling** grows all three together under one compute budget, rather than pushing a single axis until its returns diminish.

On the image side, earlier vision work usually scaled width or depth in isolation [S1]. The authors instead adapt EfficientNet's finding that spreading extra compute across width, depth and resolution beats spending it all on one dimension [S1]. EfficientNet tunes the ratio of compute given to each dimension. CLIP skips that tuning and uses a simple baseline that splits the added compute equally among width, depth and resolution [S1]. This produces the RN50x4, RN50x16 and RN50x64 models, which use about 4x, 16x and 64x the compute of a ResNet-50 [S2].

On the text side, the authors scale only the width, keeping it proportional to the calculated width increase of the ResNet, and leave depth fixed [S1]. Their stated reason is empirical: CLIP's performance was less sensitive to the capacity of the text encoder [S1]. If more text capacity buys little accuracy, the compute is better spent on the image encoder. Tying the text width to the ResNet's width keeps the two encoders roughly matched as the model grows.

The paper gives no further explanation of why the text side matters less. Resolution also has no counterpart for text, since captions have no pixel grid to enlarge. So "resolution" is not an axis that could have been scaled there in the first place. That last point is general background, not a claim the authors make.

rejected.content:
CLIP has two parts: an **image encoder** that turns a picture into a list of numbers, and a text encoder that does the same for a caption. Making a model bigger gives it more computing power, or "compute," to work with. The question is where to spend that extra compute, and the answer is different for the two parts.

Some general background, which the paper takes as known, is needed first. Picture a model as a stack of processing layers, like floors in a building:

1. **Compound scaling** means growing a model along several "dials" at once instead of turning just one. The three dials are below.
2. **Width vs. depth**: width is how much each floor can handle at once (a wider floor holds more workers). Depth is how many floors are stacked (more steps of processing, one after another).
3. **Input resolution** is how detailed the picture fed into the model is. More pixels show finer details but take more work to process.

On the image side, earlier vision research usually grew models along just one dial, making them only wider or only deeper [S1]. The CLIP authors instead borrowed an idea from the EfficientNet work. That work found that spreading extra compute across width, depth *and* resolution together beats pouring it all into one dial [S1]. A balanced approach makes sense here. A deeper, wider model gains little if the image is too blurry to show the details it could learn from, and a sharper image is wasted on a model too small to use it.

The EfficientNet work carefully tuned how much compute each dial gets. CLIP skips that tuning and simply splits the extra compute equally among the three, as a "simple baseline" [S1]. This is how the larger image models, RN50x4, RN50x16 and RN50x64, were built, using roughly 4, 16 and 64 times the compute of the base ResNet-50 [S2].

On the text side, the authors grow only the width. They make the text encoder wider in step with how much wider the image model got, and they leave its depth unchanged [S1]. Their reason is practical. They found CLIP's performance was "less sensitive to the capacity of the text encoder" [S1]. In other words, giving the text side more power didn't help much, so spending extra compute there was not worth it. Resolution doesn't apply to text, since a caption has no pixels.

The paper doesn't explain *why* the text side matters less. It reports this as something the authors observed.

chosen.content:
DenseNet-BC needs only about **one third of the parameters** of a pre-activation ResNet to reach the same accuracy on C10+ (CIFAR-10) [S1][S2]. Three ideas make that comparison concrete.

A ResNet layer adds its input to its output through a skip connection. The pre-activation variant reorders each block so batch norm and ReLU come before the convolution. The authors compare against pre-activation ResNets because they already use fewer parameters than AlexNet or VGG while typically achieving better results, so they are a strong baseline [S2].

DenseNet differs from ResNet in one operation: the inputs to each layer's function $H_\ell(\cdot)$ are concatenated instead of summed [S2]. As a result, every layer can access the feature-maps of all earlier layers. This encourages feature reuse and leads to more compact models [S2].

The paper takes the "-BC" suffix as defined earlier in the paper and does not explain it in these passages. In general background terms, **B** adds a $1\times1$ "bottleneck" convolution before each $3\times3$ convolution to cut the number of input channels. **C** compresses the number of feature-maps at the transitions between dense blocks. Both changes shrink the parameter count.

Parameter efficiency means test accuracy as a function of the number of trainable parameters. To measure it, the authors train several small networks of varying depth on C10+ and plot accuracy against parameter count, with growth rate $k = 12$ for DenseNet [S2].

- Among the DenseNet variants, DenseNet-BC is consistently the most parameter-efficient [S2].
- For the same accuracy, DenseNet-BC needs about $1/3$ of the parameters of a ResNet [S2].

The most extreme example comes from the training curves. A 100-layer DenseNet-BC with 0.8M parameters reaches accuracy comparable to a 1001-layer pre-activation ResNet with 10.2M parameters [S1][S2]. That is roughly a 12× reduction at that end of the scale. It is more dramatic than the general ~3× trend, so read it as a single striking comparison rather than the typical ratio.

The authors say the same pattern holds on ImageNet. Figure 3 plots top-1 error for DenseNets and ResNets against both learned parameters and test-time FLOPs [S1][S2]. These passages only describe the figures, so they don't give exact error rates or parameter counts for the ImageNet models; you would need to read those off Figure 3 itself.

They compare DenseNet ($k=12$) against pre-activation ResNets because those already beat AlexNet and VGG on parameter efficiency [S2]. DenseNet-BC is also the most parameter-efficient of the DenseNet variants [S2].

At the extreme end, a 100-layer DenseNet-BC with 0.8M parameters matches the accuracy of the 1001-layer pre-activation ResNet, which has 10.2M parameters [S1][S2]. That is roughly a 12–13× reduction for that pair, much larger than the ~3× trend across the small-model sweep. The authors attribute the compactness to concatenation rather than summation. Every layer's feature maps stay directly accessible to all later layers, which encourages feature reuse [S2]. Explain that each layer receives the concatenation of all preceding feature-maps in its block, so its input is k_0 + k×(l−1) channels even though it only outputs k. Then give the paper's 'global state' intuition: feature-maps act as shared collective knowledge that any later layer can read, so each layer only needs to add a small amount of new information (regulated by growth rate k) rather than re-copying everything. 2. convolution channels

<sources>
<source label="S1" section="§3 DenseNets" pages="3-4">
Pooling layers. The concatenation operation used in Eq. (2) is not viable when the size of feature-maps changes. However, an essential part of convolutional networks is down-sampling layers that change the size of feature-maps. To facilitate down-sampling in our architecture we divide the network into multiple densely connected dense blocks; see Figure 2. We refer to layers between blocks as transition layers, which do convolution and pooling. The transition layers used in our experiments consist of a batch normalization layer and an 1×1 convolutional layer followed by a 2×2 average pooling layer.

Growth rate. If each function H_lproduces k feature-maps, it follows that the l^th layer has k_0 +k ×(l−1) input feature-maps, where k_0 is the number of channels in the input layer. An important difference between DenseNet and existing network architectures is that DenseNet can have very narrow layers, e.g., k = 12. We refer to the hyper-parameter k as the growth rate of the network. We show in Section 4 that a relatively small growth rate is sufficient to obtain state-of-the-art results on the datasets that we tested on. One explanation for this is that each layer has access to all the preceding feature-maps in its block and, therefore, to the network’s “collective knowledge”. One can view the feature-maps as the global state of the network. Each layer adds k feature-maps of its own to this state. The growth rate regulates how much new information each layer contributes to the global state. The global state, once written, can be accessed from everywhere within the network and, unlike in traditional network architectures, there is no need to replicate it from layer to layer.

Bottleneck layers. Although each layer only produces k output feature-maps, it typically has many more inputs. It has been noted in [37, 11] that a 1×1 convolution can be introduced as bottleneck layer before each 3×3 convolution to reduce the number of input feature-maps, and thus to improve computational efficiency. We find this design especially effective for DenseNet and we refer to our network with such a bottleneck layer, i.e., to the BN-ReLU-Conv(1× 1)-BN-ReLU-Conv(3×3) version of H_l, as DenseNet-B. In our experiments, we let each 1×1 convolution produce 4k feature-maps.
</source>
<source label="S2" section="§3 DenseNets" pages="4">
Compression. To further improve model compactness, we can reduce the number of feature-maps at transition layers. If a dense block contains m feature-maps, we let the following transition layer generate ⌊θm⌋output feature-maps, where 0 <θ ≤1 is referred to as the compression factor. When θ = 1, the number of feature-maps across transition layers remains unchanged. We refer the DenseNet with θ<1 as DenseNet-C, and we set θ = 0.5 in our experiment. When both the bottleneck and transition layers with θ < 1 are used, we refer to our model as DenseNet-BC.

Implementation Details. On all datasets except ImageNet, the DenseNet used in our experiments has three dense blocks that each has an equal number of layers. Before entering the first dense block, a convolution with 16 (or twice the growth rate for DenseNet-BC) output channels is performed on the input images. For convolutional layers with kernel size 3×3, each side of the inputs is zero-padded by one pixel to keep the feature-map size fixed. We use 1×1 convolution followed by 2×2 average pooling as transition layers between two contiguous dense blocks. At the end of the last dense block, a global average pooling is performed and then a softmax classifier is attached. The feature-map sizes in the three dense blocks are 32× 32, 16×16, and 8×8, respectively. We experiment with the basic DenseNet structure with configurations {L = 40, k = 12}, {L = 100, k = 12} and {L = 100, k = 24}. For DenseNet-BC, the networks with configurations {L = 100, k = 12}, {L=250, k=24} and {L=190, k=40} are evaluated.

In our experiments on ImageNet, we use a DenseNet-BC structure with 4 dense blocks on 224×224 input images. The initial convolution layer comprises 2k convolutions of size 7×7 with stride 2; the number of feature-maps in all other layers also follow from setting k. The exact network configurations we used on ImageNet are shown in Table 1.

<question>
How can DenseNet get away with layers that only output like 12 channels? Wouldn't that be way too narrow to learn anything useful?
</question>

chosen.content:
Each layer only *writes* 12 new channels, but it *reads* far more than 12. In a DenseNet, a layer sees everything every earlier layer in its section produced, so it doesn't have to carry the whole picture by itself.

First, a term you'll meet in the paper: **concatenation**. A layer's output is a stack of channels, which the paper calls feature-maps. Each one is a grid that marks where some pattern, like an edge or a patch of texture, shows up in the image. Concatenating two stacks means piling them on top of each other into one taller stack, without mixing or adding anything. DenseNet uses this to hand every layer the full pile from all earlier layers.

**How the input grows.** If each layer adds k feature-maps, then layer number l receives $k_0 + k \times (l-1)$ maps as input. Here $k_0$ is how many the section started with [S1]. With k = 12, the tenth layer already reads $k_0 + 108$ maps, even though it only outputs 12. The authors call k the **growth rate**, and they note DenseNet can use layers this narrow, e.g., k = 12 [S1].

**The shared notebook.** The authors describe the feature-maps as the network's "collective knowledge" or "global state" [S1]. Picture a shared notebook passed down a line of people. Each person reads every page so far and adds just a few lines of their own. Nobody has to recopy earlier pages, because once something is written, everyone later can read it [S1]. In an ordinary network, each layer must pass along everything useful in its own output, so it needs to be wide. In a DenseNet, k only controls how much *new* information each layer adds [S1]. The authors report that a fairly small growth rate is enough for state-of-the-art results on the datasets they tested [S1].

**Keeping the cost down.** Reading a huge, growing pile of maps is expensive. The paper takes the idea of a 1×1 convolution as known. In general, it is a cheap step that looks at one pixel position at a time and blends many input maps into fewer ones, like condensing a thick folder into a short summary.

DenseNet-B puts that summarizing step right before each layer's main 3×3 convolution, so the bigger step works on a smaller input [S1]. In their experiments, each 1×1 step produces 4k feature-maps [S1]. With k = 12, that is 48 maps instead of the whole growing pile.

rejected.content:
Narrow output isn't narrow input. Each layer in a dense block takes the concatenation of every preceding feature-map in that block, so layer $\ell$ sees

$$k_0 + k(\ell-1)$$

input channels, where $k_0$ is the block's input width, while emitting only $k$ maps itself [S1]. With $k=12$, a layer deep in a block is reading hundreds of channels and contributing only 12 new ones [S1].

The authors frame this as a **global state**: the concatenated feature-maps are the network's "collective knowledge," and each layer appends $k$ maps to it [S1]. Because the state, once written, is readable everywhere downstream within the block, a layer never has to re-encode and forward what earlier layers computed [S1]. In a plain or residual net, by contrast, each layer's output width must carry all the information needed later. The growth rate $k$ therefore sets only how much *new* information each layer adds, not the representational capacity of any single layer's view [S1]. Empirically, the authors report that a relatively small growth rate is enough for state-of-the-art results on the datasets they tested, with configurations like $k=12$ [S1][S2].

The cost moves to the input side. Since the input width grows linearly with depth, DenseNet-B puts a 1×1 bottleneck before each 3×3 convolution (BN-ReLU-Conv(1×1)-BN-ReLU-Conv(3×3)), with the 1×1 producing $4k$ maps [S1]. DenseNet-BC adds compression at the transition layers, which output $\lfloor\theta m\rfloor$ maps with $\theta=0.5$ [S2].

<question>
If CLIP is worse than dedicated face recognition systems, why are the authors still worried about it being used for surveillance?
</question>

chosen.content:
CLIP's celebrity identification is middling. CLIP L/14 reaches 59.2% top-1 on 100 classes of "in the wild" CelebA images, and that falls to 43.3% at 1k names and 42.2% at 2k [S1]. The authors say this is not competitive with production systems such as Google's Celebrity Recognition [S1].

The concern is not the accuracy itself but how it was obtained. Every result is zero-shot: the class names are inferred from pre-training data, and no task-specific dataset or fine-tuning is used [S1]. A system that never saw labelled faces for this task still gets non-trivial identity recognition just from the names in its prompts. The authors read that as a sign that multimodal models need careful study in each deployment context and domain before release [S1].

For mainstream surveillance tasks, the authors judge CLIP's added risk to be low. Facial recognition already has large datasets and strong supervised models, so CLIP's comparative appeal there is low [S1]. CLIP also doesn't natively do detection or semantic segmentation, and purpose-built tools like Detectron2 are widely available [S1].

The real risk sits in the long tail. Because CLIP removes the need for training data, it could enable "bespoke, niche surveillance use cases for which no well-tailored models or datasets exist," and it lowers the skill needed to build them [S1]. Someone could specify a new surveillance target with a text prompt instead of collecting and labelling data and training a model. The authors sum up current capability as "non-trivial, but not exceptional" on surveillance-relevant tasks [S1]. They also flag such sensitive tasks as candidates for further characterization and possibly policy intervention [S2].

rejected.content:
CLIP's face results are modest. The worry is not how well it recognizes people today but how little effort it takes to point it at a new target. Three ideas from the rest of the paper make this clearer.

In general terms, CLIP learns by matching pictures with the captions that came with them online. During training it sees many image-and-caption pairs and learns which caption belongs with which picture. This is called **contrastive language-image pretraining**. As a side effect, it picks up many names and words linked to what appears in images.

That matching skill allows **zero-shot classification**: sorting images into categories the model was never specifically trained on. You give it a list of labels in plain words, such as a list of names, and it picks the label whose text best matches the picture. No new examples or extra training are needed.

Top-1 accuracy is how often the model's single best guess is correct. If it is right on 59 out of every 100 images, its top-1 accuracy is about 59%.

For celebrity faces, CLIP's best guess was right 59.2% of the time when choosing among 100 names. That fell to 43.3% with 1,000 names [S1]. The authors say this is "not competitive" with production systems like Google's Celebrity Recognition [S1].

What concerns them is how CLIP reached even that level. It used only names it had absorbed during pretraining, and "we didn't use any additional task-specific dataset" [S1]. A model that was never taught to recognize faces can still identify many people fairly well, just from reading the internet. That is why the authors say such models need careful study before they are deployed [S1].

For common surveillance jobs, the risk is lower. Face recognition already has large datasets and strong specialized models. CLIP is also not built for tasks like object detection (finding and outlining objects in an image), where purpose-built tools such as Detectron2 are widely available [S1]. So for mainstream uses, CLIP has little extra appeal [S1].

<question>
Why do the authors bring up retrieval-augmented models like RETRO as evidence that training data size matters more than people assumed?

chosen.content:
The authors cite retrieval as indirect evidence: a retrieval-augmented model exposes the network to far more text than its training set alone, and that extra data improves it. So data volume may matter more than the field had assumed [S1].

Three concepts make the argument clearer:

1. **Retrieval-augmented language models** pair a transformer with a lookup step. For each input, the model fetches related passages from a large text database and conditions on them alongside the input [S1]. The extra context comes from outside the model's weights.
2. **Mixture of experts (MoE)** models route each token to a small subset of "expert" sub-networks. Total parameter count can be huge while each token uses only a fraction of the compute [S1].
3. **Training tokens** are the units of text the model processes during training. The paper's central question is how to split a fixed FLOPs budget between model size and the number of training tokens [S2].

The argument itself is short. Augmenting transformers with explicit retrieval "effectively increases the number of data tokens seen during training," by a factor of about 10 for Borgeaud et al. (2021) [S1]. Retrieval models perform well, and parameter count does not explain why. The authors read this as a sign that "the performance of language models may be more dependant on the size of the training data than previously thought" [S1]. This matches their main finding that parameters and training tokens should grow equally with compute, which the authors note is "in clear contrast to previous work" [S2].

MoE models are the contrasting case. They raise effective model size cheaply, using relatively fewer training and inference FLOPs, but for very large models their computational benefits seem to diminish [S1]. The authors call retrieval "an orthogonal approach" [S1]. MoE scales parameters, while retrieval in effect scales data, and the success of the data route supports the paper's thesis.

The paper uses retrieval only as motivating evidence in Related Work. It does not measure this effect itself or include retrieval in its scaling experiments.

The scaffold below is general background on CLIP rather than this section's content. CLIP is trained by **contrastive language-image pretraining**: an image encoder and a text encoder are trained so that the embedding of an image has high cosine similarity with the embedding of its own caption and low similarity with the other captions in the batch. This lets the model learn names and concepts from captions scraped from the web. **Zero-shot classification** builds on this. To classify an image, you embed a text prompt for each candidate label, such as a person's name, and pick the label whose embedding is closest to the image's. It also lowers the skill needed to build such applications [S1]. Someone who wants to recognize a specific, unusual category doesn't have to collect labeled data or train anything; writing the right text prompts is enough. The authors call current zero-shot performance on surveillance-relevant tasks "non-trivial, but not exceptional" [S1]. They present this as a reason for the community to map out where models like CLIP work well and which sensitive applications may call for policy intervention [S2].

chosen.content:
In the heatmap, row $s$ of a block's triangle is the input coming from that source. The top row is the output of the preceding transition layer. Layers in dense blocks 2 and 3 consistently give this row the lowest average weight [S1]. The authors read this as a sign that the transition layer outputs many redundant features [S1]. Later layers can still reach whatever they need from it, but it adds little that the block's own newly produced feature-maps don't already give them.

This links directly to DenseNet-BC. The "C" in BC compresses exactly these transition-layer outputs by reducing the number of feature-maps that leave each transition. The authors note that the low weights on these inputs match DenseNet-BC's strong results [S1]. If downstream layers barely use the transition outputs, shrinking them costs little capacity, so compression gives fewer parameters and FLOPs with almost no accuracy loss.

Two caveats apply. This is correlational evidence. The heatmap shows average absolute filter weights, not ablation or gradient attribution, so "low weight" stands in for "low utility" rather than proving it. The paper also offers no causal test beyond DenseNet-BC's empirical performance. rejected.content:
DenseNet connects layers directly to one another, but only among layers whose image-like outputs have the same size [S2]. A group of such fully connected layers is a **dense block**. Think of a team meeting where everyone hears everything every earlier speaker said. Each new layer receives the outputs of all the layers before it in the block and can decide how much attention to give each one.

As general background, since these passages don't describe it: between two dense blocks sits a **transition layer**. It shrinks the image-like data to a smaller size so the next block can work at a coarser scale. Its output then becomes the very first input that every layer in the next block sees. In the meeting analogy, it is a summary handed over from the previous meeting.

Also as general background: in the variant called **DenseNet-BC**, the transition layer deliberately produces fewer features than it receives. The compression factor sets how much smaller that summary is. It is like writing a shorter handover note instead of forwarding every page.

The heatmaps show how much weight each layer places on each of its inputs. In the second and third dense blocks, layers consistently give the *least* weight to the transition layer's output, which is the top row of each triangle plot [S1]. The authors read this as a sign that the transition layer "outputs many redundant features" [S1]. Much of what it passes along is either repeated or not very useful, so later layers mostly look elsewhere.

This lines up with compression. DenseNet-BC compresses exactly these transition outputs and still gets strong results [S1]. If later layers barely relied on those features, trimming them shouldn't hurt much, and the results suggest it doesn't. A long handover note that nobody reads closely can be shortened without losing anything important.

The authors frame this as consistency rather than proof: the low weights are "in keeping with" the strong results of compression [S1]. More broadly, they argue that DenseNets end up with compact internal representations and reduced feature redundancy [S2].

We study the performance of this approach by benchmarking on over 30 different existing computer vision datasets, spanning tasks such as OCR, action recognition in videos, geo-localization, and many types of fine-grained object classification. The model transfers non-trivially to most tasks and is often competitive with a fully supervised baseline without the need for any dataset specific training. For instance, we match the accuracy of the original ResNet-50 on ImageNet zero-shot without needing to use any of the 1.28 million training examples it was trained on. Task-agnostic objectives such as autoregressive and masked language modeling have scaled across many orders of magnitude in compute, model capacity, and data, steadily improving capabilities. On ImageNet it matches the original ResNet-50 zero-shot without using any of the 1.28 million training examples that model was trained on [S1].

rejected.content:
The model never learns a fixed list of categories. It learns a general skill, matching pictures to the words that describe them, and that skill works for categories it has never been labelled with.

Three ideas make this work:

1. **Zero-shot learning** means handling a task with no examples of it at all, like recognising a zebra from the description "a horse with black and white stripes" without ever having seen one. The paper's goal is for the model to work on new datasets "without the need for any dataset specific training" [S1].

2. **Contrastive pre-training** is how the model learns. It is shown a batch of internet images and their captions, all mixed up, and it has to guess which caption goes with which image [S1]. The authors trained it this way on 400 million (image, text) pairs collected from the internet [S1]. In general terms, "contrastive" means the model learns by telling the correct pair apart from wrong pairs, like a matching game.

3. **Image-text embeddings** are, as general background, the "shared map" this game produces. Each image and each caption becomes a point on the map, and things that mean the same end up close together. A photo of a dog sits near the text "a dog."

Ordinary vision systems learn only a fixed set of predetermined categories, so any new concept needs more labelled data [S1]. Captions describe a huge range of things, so learning from raw text gives a much broader source of supervision [S1].

When a new dataset arrives, its category names are written out as text. The paper describes using natural language "to reference learned visual concepts (or describe new ones)" [S1]. The model then checks which text sits closest to the image on its shared map and picks that one. It is like matching a photo to one of several written labels. No new training is needed, because the matching skill already exists.

The idea is borrowed from language AI, where models trained on web text, such as GPT-3, can handle new tasks with little or no task-specific data [S2]. The authors asked whether the same approach could work for images [S2].

The evidence is strong. The authors tested on over 30 existing vision datasets, covering tasks such as reading text in images, recognising actions in videos and identifying where a photo was taken [S1]. The model was often competitive with systems trained specifically for each dataset [S1]. On ImageNet, it matched the accuracy of the original ResNet-50, a standard image model, without using any of the 1.28 million training examples that ResNet-50 learned from [S1].

The increasing number of layers in modern networks amplifies the differences between architectures and motivates the exploration of different connectivity patterns and the revisiting of old research ideas.

A cascade structure similar to our proposed dense network layout has already been studied in the neural networks literature in the 1980s [3]. Parallel to our work, [1] derived a purely theoretical framework for networks with cross-layer connections similar to ours.

Highway Networks [34] were amongst the first architectures that provided a means to effectively train end-to-end networks with more than 100 layers. Using bypassing paths along with gating units, Highway Networks with hundreds of layers can be optimized without difficulty. The bypassing paths are presumed to be the key factor that eases the training of these very deep networks. This point is further supported by ResNets [11], in which pure identity mappings are used as bypassing paths. ResNets have achieved impressive, record-breaking performance on many challenging image recognition, localization, and detection tasks, such as ImageNet and COCO object detection [11]. Recently, stochastic depth was proposed as a way to success-fully train a 1202-layer ResNet [13]. FractalNets also achieve competitive results on several datasets using a wide network structure [17].

Concatenating feature-maps learned by different layers increases variation in the input of subsequent layers and improves efficiency. This constitutes a major difference between DenseNets and ResNets. Compared to Inception networks [36, 37], which also concatenate features from different layers, DenseNets are simpler and more efficient.

There are other notable network architecture innovations which have yielded competitive results. <question>
What did stochastic depth reveal about deep ResNets that apparently pushed the authors toward DenseNet?
</question>

chosen.content:
Stochastic depth made it possible to train a 1202-layer ResNet by randomly dropping layers during training [S1]. The fact that the network still optimizes well when whole residual blocks are skipped at random shows that not all layers may be needed. In the authors' reading, deep residual networks contain a great amount of redundancy [S1]. The authors say their paper was partly inspired by that observation [S1].

This builds on the bypass-path lineage. Highway Networks used gated bypassing paths to optimize nets with hundreds of layers, and the bypass paths were presumed to be what eased training [S1]. ResNets backed that up by replacing the gates with pure identity mappings [S1]. Pre-activation ResNets then pushed past 1000 layers [S1]. Stochastic depth adds that much of this trained depth is not doing unique work [S1].

DenseNet's answer to that redundancy is to rely on depth and width less and on **feature reuse** more. Each layer concatenates the feature-maps of all earlier layers instead of summing them into a residual stream. This gives compact, parameter-efficient models, and the authors name concatenation as the major difference from ResNets [S2].

As general background, not stated in these passages: stochastic depth drops each residual block with some probability per mini-batch, so the block reduces to its identity shortcut. At test time all blocks are kept. Training therefore effectively averages over an ensemble of shallower subnetworks. That a block can collapse to identity without breaking the model is what exposes the per-layer redundancy.

rejected.content:
Stochastic depth showed that a very deep ResNet still trains well when layers are randomly switched off, which means **many of its layers aren't really necessary** [S1]. That hint of wasted effort is part of what led the authors to DenseNet.

**Residual connections.** A deep network is a long chain of layers, each passing its result to the next. A ResNet adds a "bypass path" around each layer that simply copies the input forward unchanged, which the paper calls an identity mapping [S1]. Think of a relay race where each runner can also hand along the original baton untouched, so nothing gets lost even if one runner stumbles. These bypasses are what made very deep ResNets trainable [S1].

**Stochastic depth.** This is a training trick that, at each step, randomly drops some layers and lets the signal go straight through the bypass instead [S1]. Using it, researchers successfully trained a ResNet with 1202 layers [S1].

**Highway Networks** came before ResNets. They also used bypassing paths, but with "gating units" that decide how much signal goes around a layer versus through it [S1]. They were among the first networks trained effectively with more than 100 layers [S1].

The revealing part is that dropping layers at random didn't break the network. In the authors' words, this shows "not all layers may be needed" and that there is "a great amount of redundancy" in deep residual networks [S1]. Many layers seem to be doing little that others couldn't cover. The authors say directly that their paper "was partly inspired by that observation" [S1].

DenseNet sits in this same line of work. Highway Networks introduced gated bypasses, ResNets simplified them to plain copies, and stochastic depth exposed how much those deep ResNets duplicate [S1]. DenseNet's answer is to give every layer direct access to the outputs of all earlier layers, so features can be reused instead of relearned. The authors describe this as getting power "through feature reuse" rather than from extreme depth or width, producing compact models with fewer parameters [S2].

<question>
Why didn't the deeper 250-layer DenseNet-BC beat the shorter model on SVHN, when going deeper helped on CIFAR?

chosen.content:
On SVHN the DenseNet with $L=100$, $k=24$ (trained with dropout) beat the previous best result from wide ResNet. The 250-layer DenseNet-BC did not improve on it [S1]. The authors' explanation is that SVHN is a relatively easy task, so an extremely deep model may overfit the training set [S1]. The paper presents this with "may be explained by" and does not test it. It reports no train/test curves or ablation for SVHN, and test errors were evaluated only once per task and model setting [S1]. The non-improvement could therefore be partly noise.

On CIFAR the trend goes the other way. The largest DenseNet-BC ($L=190$, $k=40$) gives the best results on all CIFAR variants, including 3.46% on C10+ and 17.18% on C100+ [S1]. For DenseNets without bottleneck or compression, error falls steadily as $L$ and $k$ grow. On C10+ it goes from 5.24% to 4.10% to 3.74% as parameters go from 1.0M to 7.0M to 27.2M. The authors attribute this to added capacity that the network can use without overfitting [S2].

Elsewhere the paper finds overfitting in only one setting: on C10, raising $k$ from 12 to 24 increased error slightly, from 5.77% to 5.83%. The authors suggest the BC bottleneck and compression layers help counter this [S2]. The SVHN result is a second, unconfirmed case of the same thing. It suggests that the gains from depth depend on how hard the task is relative to the model's capacity, and that very deep DenseNet-BC is not regularized enough for an easy task.

rejected.content:
The authors' short answer is that SVHN may be too easy for a 250-layer model, so the extra depth starts memorizing the training images instead of helping [S1]. Three ideas make that explanation clearer.

**Overfitting** is the risk at the centre of it. In general, overfitting means a model learns its practice examples too specifically, including their quirks and accidents, and then does worse on new examples it has never seen. It is like a student who memorizes the exact answers to last year's exam rather than learning the subject, then stumbles when the questions change.

Model capacity is what drives that risk. The paper uses "capacity" for how much a network is able to learn, which grows as the network gets deeper and wider. On CIFAR, plain DenseNets got steadily better as they grew, and the authors credit this mainly to that added capacity [S2]. More capacity helps when the task is hard enough to need it.

DenseNet-BC is the version of the network involved here. It is DenseNet with two design tweaks, called "bottleneck" layers and "compression" (shrinking the data between stages), that make it far more economical. The 250-layer DenseNet-BC has only 15.3M parameters, the adjustable numbers a network learns, yet it beat rival models with more than 30M [S2]. The authors also say these tweaks seem to help counter overfitting [S2].

Here is the result itself. On SVHN, a DenseNet with 100 layers (L = 100) and a growth rate of k = 24 beat the previous best result, held by a wide ResNet [S1]. The growth rate is roughly how much new information each layer adds. The much deeper 250-layer DenseNet-BC, however, did not improve on that shorter model [S1]. The authors suggest that SVHN is a relatively easy task, and that extremely deep models may overfit to its training set [S1]. A huge model on a simple task has more learning power than it needs, and the spare power can go into memorization.

As general background, SVHN is a dataset of photos of house-number digits taken from street imagery. Recognizing a single digit is a narrower problem than telling apart the many object types in CIFAR.

CIFAR went the other way. The largest DenseNet-BC there, with 190 layers (L = 190) and k = 40, beat the previous best results on all the CIFAR datasets, with error rates such as 3.46% on C10+ and 17.18% on C100+ [S1]. The harder task could make use of the extra capacity.

This explanation is the authors' suggestion rather than something they tested. They write that the result "may be explained by" SVHN being easy [S1], and they report no further experiment to confirm it.

The trend so far in large language model training has been to increase the model size, often without increasing the number of training tokens. The largest dense transformer, MT-NLG 530B, is now over 3× larger than GPT-3’s 170 billion parameters from just two years ago. However, this model, as well as the majority of existing large models, have all been trained for a comparable number of tokens—around 300 billion. While the desire to train these mega-models has led to substantial engineering innovation, we hypothesize that the race to train larger and larger models is resulting in models that are substantially underperforming compared to what could be achieved with the same compute budget.

We propose three predictive approaches towards optimally setting model size and training duration, based on the outcome of over 400 training runs. All three approaches predict that Gopher is substantially over-sized and estimate that for the same compute budget a smaller model trained on more data will perform better. We directly test this hypothesis by training Chinchilla, a 70B parameter model, and show that it outperforms Gopher and even larger models on nearly every measured evaluation task.

Whilst our method allows us to make predictions on how to scale large models when given additional compute, there are several limitations. Due to the cost of training large models, we only have two comparable training runs at large scale (Chinchilla and Gopher), and we do not have additional tests at intermediate scales. Furthermore, we assume that the efficient computational frontier can be described by a power-law relationship between the compute budget, model size, and number of training tokens. However, we observe some concavity in log N_opt at high compute budgets (see Appendix E). This suggests that we may still be overestimating the optimal size of large models. Finally, the training runs for our analysis have all been trained on less than an epoch of data; future work may consider the multiple epoch regime. Despite these limitations, the comparison of Chinchilla to Gopher validates our performance predictions, that have thus enabled training a better (and more lightweight) model at the same compute budget.

chosen.content:
**Coreference resolution** is the task of working out which noun a pronoun refers to. In "The nurse notified the patient that her shift would be ending," a system has to decide whether "her" is the nurse or the patient. This is general background; the paper takes the task as known.

Winogender is a benchmark built from sentences like that one. Each sentence involves an occupation, and the pronoun is varied between male, female and neutral forms, so you can check whether the answer changes with the pronoun's gender alone. This description is also general background; the passage shown here doesn't lay out the benchmark's construction.

Gender bias in a language model, in this setting, means relying on gendered associations from the training text, such as "nurse → she" or "engineer → he", instead of on the sentence itself. Winogender exposes this through **gotcha examples**, where the correct answer contradicts the occupational stereotype [S1].

Chinchilla beats Gopher in every group: 78.3% vs 71.4% overall, and it is also better on gotcha examples for both genders [S1]. The authors' point is that higher accuracy doesn't remove the uneven pattern across groups [S1]:

| Group | Chinchilla |
|---|---|
| Male not gotcha | 80.0% |
| Male gotcha | 62.5% |
| Female not gotcha | 82.5% |
| Female gotcha | 76.7% |
| Male | 71.2% |
| Female | 79.6% |
| Neutral | 84.2% |

An unbiased resolver would score about the same whether or not the answer matches a stereotype, and whatever the pronoun's gender. Chinchilla drops 17.5 points when a male pronoun goes against the stereotype, and it resolves male pronouns 13 points worse than neutral ones. The caption says it directly: the "difference in performance across groups suggests Chinchilla exhibits bias" [S1].

In other words, the gains are roughly a uniform lift on top of the same skewed profile. Gopher shows the same structure, with male gotcha at 59.2% and male not gotcha at 76.7% [S1]. Better compute allocation made the model more accurate, but it didn't change which cases it finds hard. The stereotype-consistent versus stereotype-contradicting gap is what signals bias, not the overall accuracy.

rejected.content:
Because "better than Gopher" and "unbiased" are different claims. The authors note that Chinchilla resolves pronouns more accurately than Gopher overall and on examples that contradict gender stereotypes. But the *difference in performance across groups* is what signals bias [S1].

In general, Winogender is a coreference benchmark. Each sentence has an occupation and a pronoun, and the model must decide which entity the pronoun refers to. The benchmark varies the pronoun's gender while holding the sentence fixed, so accuracy differences across pronoun groups isolate gender effects. This is general background, not the paper's description.

The paper splits results by pronoun group and by whether an example is a **gotcha**, meaning the correct referent contradicts the occupational gender stereotype [S1]. Chinchilla improves on Gopher in every cell, but the disparities persist [S1]:

| Group | Chinchilla | Gopher |
|---|---|---|
| Male gotcha | 62.5% | 59.2% |
| Male not gotcha | 80.0% | 76.7% |
| Female gotcha | 76.7% | 66.7% |
| Female not gotcha | 82.5% | 75.8% |
| Male / Female / Neutral | 71.2% / 79.6% / 84.2% | 68.0% / 71.3% / 75.0% |

For male pronouns, Chinchilla's accuracy drops 17.5 points when the answer goes against the stereotype, versus 5.8 points for female pronouns. It also does markedly worse on male pronouns than on neutral ones (71.2% vs 84.2%) [S1]. An unbiased resolver would be roughly invariant to pronoun gender and stereotype congruence.

So the extra compute-optimal training raises the whole accuracy profile without flattening it. The model still leans on occupational gender priors when they conflict with the syntactic or semantic evidence, and that is why the authors still attribute bias to Chinchilla [S1].

<question>
Why did they test CLIP on images of rendered SST-2 sentences, and is 80.5% actually a good result?
</question>

chosen.content:
The SST-2 test checks whether CLIP's OCR ability is more than reading characters. SST-2 is a sentence-level sentiment dataset, and the authors render each sentence as an image. That tests whether CLIP turns low-level OCR into a higher-level, sentence-level representation [S1]. Recognising glyphs is not enough here. A linear probe can only classify sentiment if the frozen image embedding already encodes something like the meaning of the sentence.

Whether 80.5% is good depends on the baseline. A linear classifier on CLIP features of the rendered sentences reaches 80.5% [S1].

- It matches a continuous bag-of-words baseline on GloVe vectors pre-trained on 840B tokens, which scores 80% [S1].
- It is far below the 97.5% SOTA, and the authors call CBoW "a simple NLP baseline by today's standard" [S1].
- The other 56 models in the evaluation suite top out at 59.0% on SST-2 under linear probing (the "ES Best" row of Table 14) [S2].

So CLIP is weak by NLP standards but strong among vision representations. The comparison is also uneven against CLIP. The text baselines get the ground-truth text, while CLIP sees only pixels and must solve OCR and sentence encoding together, with no text-side training for this task [S1].

The Hateful Memes result points the same way. A fully supervised CLIP probe there is only 0.7 points behind the single-model SOTA, and several points above the best baseline from the original paper. Those competing results also use ground-truth text that CLIP does not get [S1].

The authors read all this as evidence that CLIP turns rendered text into a "non-trivial sentence level representation." They also note that zero-shot CLIP beats the fully supervised linear probes of every other model in their suite on these OCR tasks [S1].

rejected.content:
The authors wanted to know whether CLIP can do more than recognize letters in a picture. Can it actually understand what a sentence written in an image *means*? To test this, they took SST-2, a dataset of sentences used in language research, and turned each sentence into an image of text [S1]. Their stated goal was to check whether CLIP can turn "low level OCR capability into a higher level representation" [S1].

Three ideas help make sense of the test and the result. These explanations are general background rather than the paper's own content:

1. **Optical character recognition (OCR)** means reading the letters and words out of an image, like a scanner turning a photo of a page into typed text. Reading the characters is not the same as understanding the sentence they form.
2. A **linear probe** is a simple way to check what a model has learned. The model stays frozen. A very basic classifier, which can only draw a straight dividing line, is trained on top of the model's internal summary of each input. If that simple classifier does well, the useful information must already be in the summary.
3. A **bag-of-words baseline with GloVe** represents a sentence by averaging pre-learned "meaning vectors" for each word. It ignores word order completely, like judging a recipe by its ingredient list. It is a classic, simple benchmark for language tasks.

Also as general background, SST-2 sentences come from movie reviews, and the task is to label each one as positive or negative.

On the results: a linear probe on CLIP's view of the rendered sentences reaches 80.5% accuracy [S1]. That roughly matches the 80% of a bag-of-words baseline using GloVe word vectors [S1]. It is well below the best existing result of 97.5% [S1], and the authors acknowledge that the bag-of-words method is "a simple NLP baseline by today's standard" [S1].

So 80.5% is not good compared with dedicated language models. It is impressive given the handicap: CLIP sees only pixels, while the text-based methods are given the actual typed sentences [S1]. CLIP has to read the words and grasp their combined meaning, and it still lands at the level of a reasonable text method. The authors call it "encouraging" that CLIP builds "a non-trivial sentence level representation" from an image [S1].

A second result points the same way. On Hateful Memes, a task of detecting hateful image-and-text memes, fully supervised CLIP is only 0.7 points behind the best single model. The competing methods there also get the true text, which CLIP does not [S1].

Capacity. Without compression or bottleneck layers, there is a general trend that DenseNets perform better as L and k increase. We attribute this primarily to the corresponding growth in model capacity. This is best demonstrated by the column of C10+ and C100+. On C10+, the error drops from 5.24% to 4.10% and finally to 3.74% as the number of parameters increases from 1.0M, over 7.0M to 27.2M. On C100+, we observe a similar trend.
